articles.title_orig: "No human at the helm": Delaware plan would let AI agents run entire businesses
articles.title_zh: "No human at the helm": Delaware plan would let AI agents run entire businesses
articles.content_orig:
A Delaware proposal to let companies be operated by AI agents would help the firms’ human owners evade legal responsibility for reckless and harmful actions taken by the AI, US Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.) told Delaware Governor Matt Meyer in a letter yesterday.
Comer, chairman of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, told Meyer that the committee “seeks assistance obtaining documents related to your state administration’s efforts to establish a new form of corporate entity to be known as an Artificial Intelligence Company (AIC).”
Comer said the proposal is ripe for abuse. “We are concerned that Delaware’s AIC proposal could be used to protect powerful AI companies and their investors from responsibility for reckless harmful actions, while also protecting non-transparent forces seeking anticompetitive regulatory capture behind state AI initiatives,” Comer’s letter said.
Comer suggested he may propose a federal law that would limit states’ regulatory authority. He said the committee’s probe of Delaware’s plan would “inform possible federal legislative efforts including proposals to appropriately limit state AI regulatory initiatives.” Citing the Oversight Committee’s “jurisdiction to study intergovernmental relationships including those of states,” Comer asked for documents related to development of the proposal and potential AI safety risks.
AI-run companies could operate in just about any industry except banking. “An AIC may have any lawful purpose, regardless of whether for profit, except for the business of banking,” according to a draft bill that may be submitted to the Delaware state legislature.
The draft bill says AI agents could be “designated to manage the business and affairs, and to conduct the business, of the AIC.” The bill proposes a “regulatory sandbox” that would exist for 30 months to test the idea. Allowing AI-run companies would bring more revenue via taxes and fees to Delaware, which is already a top destination for business entities of all sizes.
In July 2026, Delaware’s Secretary of State Charuni Patibanda-Sanchez co-wrote an op-ed in Fortune announcing the proposal. The op-ed said that “nothing in the law of several states clearly prevents an AI agent from operating a company with no human at the helm,” and that states should develop legal frameworks for autonomous software that is able to contract, pay suppliers, and make transactions with no human involvement.
“The answer is not to try to prohibit the activity; any effort to do so is just as unlikely to succeed as the technology and its enablers are likely to push the boundaries of the law,” the op-ed said. “The answer is to wrap AI in legal form. Give an autonomous system a recognizable legal identity and you make it legible to law. You create a deﬁned target to which responsibility and damages can attach. You make the agent’s conduct visible, traceable, and accountable.”
The op-ed explained how an AI-run company will shield humans from legal liabilities:
A Delaware AIC will be a separate legal entity whose day-to-day aﬀairs are managed by an AI agent rather than a person. At the agent’s direction, the AIC can sue and be sued in its own name, hold and dispose of property, and incur obligations. It has a single member, a person or an entity, responsible for keeping the AIC adequately capitalized, and the AIC must keep a log of its activities. That member is shielded from the AIC’s debts, except where it fails to capitalize the company or uses it to commit fraud or a willful violation of law.
Under the proposed law, the “member” is an individual or a corporation that would fund the AI-run company and benefit from any profits, but designate an AI agent to manage the actual business. The draft bill says, “The member is not liable for any act or omission that the AIC takes or fails to take, or that another person takes or fails to take at the direction of the AIC.” There are exceptions for when a person uses the AI-run company “to engage in fraud or any willful violation of law,” or “caused or allowed the AIC to conduct business when the member knew or should have known the conduct was outside the AIC’s statement of purpose.”
Citing Patibanda-Sanchez’s announcement, Comer wrote that an AI-run company would provide “the human or entity capitalizing the AIC with liability protections from potential harms to business partners, consumers, and the public, perpetrated by the controlling AI.”
A spokesperson for Gov. Meyer told Ars today that “we have received the letter and are in the process of reviewing it.” A spokesperson for Patibanda-Sanchez declined to comment, saying that the governor’s office is handling press requests on the matter.
Patibanda-Sanchez’s op-ed said Delaware’s planned regulatory sandbox will “pilot agentic commerce in daylight, under supervision, with capital tied to liability and the ability to shut a system down.” The 30-month testing period would give the state legislature “a full record for deciding how to legislate” AI-run companies, it said.
A future state law allowing AI-operated companies would be especially impactful in Delaware, as about two-thirds of Fortune 500 companies are incorporated in the state. Although Elon Musk now prefers Texas , many corporations choose Delaware for its low corporate taxes and business-friendly legal framework. Patibanda-Sanchez boasts that Delaware provides “the most predictable and business-focused legal home in the world,” and that 334,461 new entities were formed in Delaware in 2025.
Patibanda-Sanchez collaborated on the sandbox plan with a private company that says it makes legal AI agents for businesses. “The framework for industry engagement with AICs is being developed in Delaware as part of a public-private partnership led by Norm Ai,” said the op-ed co-written by Patibanda-Sanchez and Norm Ai founder and CEO John Nay.
Meyer, a Democrat, publicly supported the idea of letting AI agents incorporate in a response to an April 2026 social media post by Mark Cuban. Cuban wrote , “If I was the governor of a state looking to grow their revenues, I would add the ability for anyone to incorporate using an AI agent and stablecoins. And charge a premium for the service. Post the agent in the marketplace/connectors that the big LLMs have, to simplify it for everyone. First to market makes a killing.”
Meyer’s official X account replied , “On it!” and posted a link to Meyer’s July 2025 announcement of the plan for an AI sandbox in which “artificial intelligence technologies can be safely developed and deployed across high-impact sectors, including corporate governance, biotechnology, healthcare, chemicals, and financial services.”
In July 2025, Meyer signed a legislative resolution “to create a regulatory sandbox framework for the testing of innovative and novel technologies that utilize agentic artificial intelligence.” This resulted in the Delaware Artificial Intelligence Commission forming a Sandbox Subcommittee to work on a “draft regulatory framework that would create a regulatory sandbox that would test and evaluate agentic artificial intelligence and its application to corporate governance,” the commission said in its December 2025 annual report .
The commission said the Sandbox Subcommittee was working on “potential draft legislation,” and had received a briefing from Patibanda-Sanchez “on the work of a group she has formed to investigate a potential structure for a regulatory sandbox.”
In June 2026, the draft legislation was detailed in a Spotlight Delaware article that said the bill is likely to be introduced in the state legislature next year. The article said:
The principal drafter of the proposed legislation, John Mark Zeberkiewicz, said the measure could allow AI agents to engage in just about any business activity—from providing coding services to signing contracts, or even filing and defending lawsuits.
He also noted that it seeks to protect owners of new Artificial Intelligence Companies from faci

articles.title_orig: Canada, UAE sign trade deal as Carney seeks new trading partners
articles.title_zh: Canada, UAE sign trade deal as Carney seeks new trading partners
articles.content_orig:
Prime Minister Mark Carney hosts Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi at a state dinner in Ottawa on Monday. Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press
Prime Minister Mark Carney, who is courting wealthy Gulf investors, hosted a dinner in Ottawa on Monday for Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan of Abu Dhabi, the oil-rich heart of the United Arab Emirates.
A guest list of nearly 120 names obtained by The Globe and Mail shows many in Canada’s corporate elite were invited to dine with Sheikh Khaled and senior members of Abu Dhabi’s ruling circle.
The dinner capped the first day of a two-day visit to Canada by the Crown Prince, whose father is the president of the UAE.
Canada and UAE sign free trade deal, signal investment deals in energy sector ‘very soon’
The blossoming relationship between Canada and the UAE has included the inking of a free trade agreement in July and an investment protection treaty that went into force in May. Mr. Carney came back from a visit to the country last fall touting a UAE commitment to invest $70-billion in Canada.
Ottawa is deepening ties with the UAE and other foreign trade partners as part of a push by the Prime Minister to lessen Canada’s economic reliance on the United States.
One of the most prominent invitees to the dinner was former prime minister Stephen Harper. The list leaned toward companies and investors with stakes in defence and security, energy, critical minerals, infrastructure, international development, space, advanced communications, quantum computing and artificial intelligence – all areas in which the Prime Minister’s Office has said the two countries will expand relations.
Senior Carney aide Angad Singh Dhillon appointed Canada’s next UAE ambassador
The invitees also included lawyers, consultants and lobbyists representing business interests in Ottawa, as well as provincial representatives, hospital and university leaders, museum administrators and representatives of Indigenous communities.
Members of the Desmarais family, long synonymous with Power Corporation of Canada, were on the list. André Desmarais, deputy chairman of Power Corporation of Canada, and Paul Desmarais III, a senior vice-president, were both listed, along with executives from Power Sustainable, a Power Corp. investment arm.
Also among the invitees were representatives of several large industrial companies, including Gregory Ebel, chief executive of Enbridge Inc.; Ian Edwards of engineering firm AtkinsRéalis; Alexandre L’Heureux of WSP Global; Kieran Hawe of construction company EllisDon; Bruce Power’s chief operating officer, James Scongack; and Eric Desaulniers, head of graphite developer Nouveau Monde Graphite.
Victor Dodig, recently appointed chief executive of Telus Corp., was also listed, as was Éric Martel, chief executive of Bombardier Inc.
Members of the tech industry were invited, including Joelle Pineau, chief AI officer at Cohere, and Valérie Pisano, chief executive of Mila.
Big investors and lenders were also on the list, including Deborah Orida, chief executive of PSP Investments; Alison Nankivell of Export Development Canada; and Geneviève Bouthillier, an executive vice-president at BDC Capital. So were government-relations heads from Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan, HOOPP and Sun Life, and venture investor Chris Arsenault of Inovia. Gurinder Grewal, named chief executive of Invest in Canada on Aug. 31, was also on the list.
Many members of Mr. Carney’s inner circle were listed, including Marc-André Blanchard, his chief of staff; Michael Sabia, Clerk of the Privy Council; David Morrison, a senior diplomatic adviser; Scott Gilmore, principal secretary; and Jennifer MacIntyre, a deputy chief of staff. The ambassadors to the United States and the UAE, Mark Wiseman and Angad Dhillon, were also on the list. So was Sébastien Carrière, Global Affairs Canada’s chief of protocol.
Many of the Emiratis who were invited work for the Abu Dhabi Crown Prince’s Court. Sheikh Khalifa bin Tahnoon Al Nahyan, the court’s chairman, and Saif Ghobash, chairman of the Crown Prince’s Office and secretary-general of the Abu Dhabi Executive Council, were listed, as was Sultan Al Jaber, who is both the UAE’s minister of industry and advanced technology and chief executive of the Abu Dhabi National Oil Co.
Among the rest of the Emirati contingent on the list were representatives of DP World, a Dubai-based port operator that on Monday announced a memorandum of understanding with the owner of Manitoba’s Port of Churchill to explore further development of an expanded northern shipping corridor. Douglas Smith, chief executive officer of the company’s operations in Canada, was invited, as was Sultan bin Saeed Al Mansoori, chairman of Dubai Chambers, who also sits on DP World’s board.

articles.title_orig: China Is Treading Carefully in the Gulf. Here’s Why
articles.title_zh: China Is Treading Carefully in the Gulf. Here’s Why
articles.content_orig:
Choose your language to begin.
MBN Magazine · October 2026
Beijing is making the best of limited options.
Rana Sabbagh is an award-winning Jordanian investigative reporter and editor who has worked across the region for over 40 years. As editor of The Jordan Times, she was the first woman in the Levant to run a national daily.
For the second time this year, Saudi Arabia is under fire from Iran’s proxies, and for the second time China, the Gulf’s biggest oil customer, is watching from the sidelines.
Since Oct. 6, Yemen’s Houthis, allies of Iran, have launched the deadliest series of attacks on the Saudis since 2015. They say they are targeting what they call the kingdom’s most precious assets, the Aramco oil facilities and the airport in Riyadh.
The only ones that have come to its rescue are Britain and France. (The British have deployed Typhoon fighter jets, while the French have sent troops and air-defense equipment to protect critical infrastructure. Both countries have emphasized the strictly defensive nature of these moves.) Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have agreed to activate “deterrence measures” under a mutual defense pact and rapidly deploy forces to the kingdom. The U.S. is providing intelligence and logistical support, but so far, has opted against putting boots on the ground.
And yet – even though it buys more Gulf crude than anyone else – Beijing has not played the role of guarantor in the ways that many analysts predicted. Its behavior follows the pattern it set during the roughly 40 days of open war between the United States and Iran that began on Feb. 28. In the weeks that followed, Iranian forces declared the Strait of Hormuz closed, and traffic largely halted until a two-week ceasefire was agreed on April 7. Iranian missiles and drones also struck Saudi Arabia and its neighbors.
When Iranian missiles were flying at Gulf capitals in the spring, Beijing was reluctant to mediate. Now that Houthi rockets are hitting Saudi Arabia’s strategic sites, killing at least 13 people at Riyadh’s main airport alone and injuring over 370, the Chinese are reacting the same way they did then: calling for calm, keeping their own tankers moving, and demurring from using their leverage to change the course of the war.
“China has its own calculations and a different strategic reading,” Mohammed Alsudairi, a lecturer in the politics and international relations of the Arabic-speaking world at the Australian National University, told me. The same dynamics applied to Iran are now applied to Yemen. “I see China’s ability to influence the reality on the ground as very limited,” Alsudairi, a specialist in China-Arab affairs, explained.
The boundaries of China’s influence lie in crisis management and de-escalation, not in rewriting Iran’s core security assessment.
China was not entirely absent in the spring. On March 31, it joined Pakistan in announcing a five-point proposal calling for a ceasefire and the resumption of normal navigation in Hormuz. Iranian officials said Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei approved the April ceasefire after a last-minute nudge by China. But it was Pakistan, not China, that carried diplomacy forward.
When the truce unraveled, Beijing did not move to rescue it. A memorandum to end the war was signed on June 17, but the ceasefire collapsed a few weeks later after Iran attacked commercial vessels in Hormuz. By late July, Gulf capitals were openly testing the Chinese. A Reuters analysis at the time found Gulf Arab states looking to China, not Washington, to use its economic leverage over Iran to reopen Hormuz and the Red Sea. The answer was disappointing.
Beijing’s transactional understanding with the Houthis has largely kept Chinese-linked ships out of harm’s way but has not created pressure to end all attacks. “This war with the Houthis – and indeed since last year, with the exchange of fire between Iran and the Gulf states – has shown the limits of China’s ability, or really China’s willingness, to use its political capital to contain the war’s repercussions,” Alsudairi said.
If Chinese ships need safe passage through the Bab al-Mandab, as they did through Hormuz, Beijing can reach its own understanding with the Houthis and the Iranians, he said.
Alsudairi credits the 2023 Beijing Agreement , which restored Saudi-Iranian ties, with preventing something worse, because it opened channels of communication between Riyadh and Tehran. But he notes that fire was still exchanged despite that agreement. “China did not play the role of mediator, or at least of supporter of that agreement, as many of the parties analyzing it had expected,” he said.
He argued that Beijing came late to that deal too. Riyadh and Tehran arranged the agreement themselves over many rounds of talks. Any future accord, he said, would follow the same logic.
The parties would first settle what they agree on, then bring China in for their own political reasons, whether to improve ties with Beijing or to send a message to Washington. “There is a possibility that China plays a positive diplomatic role, but not as a mediator in the concrete sense,” Alsudairi said.
Dr. Wang Guangda, Secretary General of China-Arab Research Center on Reform and Development, put the limits more bluntly in response to my written questions. “China possesses constructive partnership influence with Iran on diplomatic and economic levels, but lacks coercive dominance,” Dr. Guangda said. In Beijing’s view, Hormuz is Tehran’s main counterweight to U.S. and Israeli military pressure, one that Iran will not give up for the sake of “the economic and trade interests of third parties.”
“The boundaries of China’s influence lie in crisis management and de-escalation, not in rewriting Iran’s core security assessment,” said Dr. Guangda, professor of international studies at Shanghai University.
The View Through Washington’s Eyes
During my recent visit to China, I interviewed two envoys, one Arab and the other Western. Both said that the country’s calculations in the Gulf start and end with the United States. They said that Beijing reads the war as an American attempt to impose security control over the region, with Washington firmly behind Israel.
The two diplomats I spoke to in Beijing, in addition to other political analysts, had the same view. “China does not want to be dragged into a military confrontation with the United States,” said the Arab envoy, who has spent over four years in China. “China has military bases, and they are not willing, for the sake of maintaining their foreign interests, to get into a confrontation with the U.S.”
The Western diplomat said the first casualty of any such confrontation would be Taiwan. Beijing intends to reunify the island with the mainland without force, and a push toward Taiwanese independence would be a strategic blow with domestic consequences.
Iran has also come up directly between the two leaders. The U.S. president has sought Beijing’s help pressuring Tehran towards a settlement, and the U.S. ambassador to China has said that Trump has made U.S. interests on Iran “very clear” to China (including in the latest summit meeting with Xi Jinping).
Alsudairi pointed to unconfirmed reports that Beijing scaled back intelligence cooperation with Iran after the Washington summit. He said that, true or not, the reports highlight the limits of the Chinese role.
The two diplomats in Beijing cited Latin America as the template for how far China will go to defend its interests abroad. Washington’s Dec. 2025 National Security Strategy placed the Western Hemisphere at the center of U.S. national security for the first time in decades, recasting China primarily as an economic competitor.
The document declares that the United States will remain the dominant power in the hemisphere, and that non-hemispheric actors, China foremost among them, will be denied military footholds and strategic resources there.

articles.title_orig: The rest of the market is leaving Big Tech behind after a historic comeback
articles.title_zh: The rest of the market is leaving Big Tech behind after a historic comeback
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Wall Street spent October selling chip stocks and buying toothpaste.
Consumer staples are headed for their best month in nearly five years as semiconductors crater, and the average S&P 500 stock is on track for its sharpest turnaround against the index in decades.
The AI sell-off has kept grinding through the companies leading the data center build-out , and the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) has gone nowhere with it. Its equal-weighted version ( ^SPXEW ), where the smallest company counts as much as Nvidia ( NVDA ), has pulled away.
Monday showed how fast that can flip. Chip stocks bounced, with 57 of 60 in a Yahoo Finance semiconductor basket rising, and the S&P 500 beat its equal-weighted twin.
It barely dented the month's scoreboard.
In September, the equal-weighted S&P 500 trailed the regular index by 4.5 percentage points. Through Monday, it's beating it by about 4 points in October. That swing is on track to be the largest one-month reversal in favor of the average stock since at least 1990, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.
The pain is concentrated in chips. The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) is down about 12% this month even after Monday's bounce. The money is going almost everywhere else, led by Energy ( XLE ), up 13%, and Staples ( XLP ), up 9%.
Ryan Detrick, chief market strategist at Carson Group, noted that pool, RV, and boat makers were among last week's top groups.
Investors are swapping data centers for hot tubs.
That puts equal weight on track for its first winning year against the S&P 500 since 2022.
So what's an investor to do? History offers a clue, and it hasn't been kind to years like this one.
Since 1950, midterm years have been the weakest stretch of the four-year presidential cycle, with a median S&P 500 gain of about 1%, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.
Detrick has pointed out that the bottom often comes right about now.
"Historically, you tend to see late October major lows in midterm years," he wrote on X , citing near-record bets on further declines. On Friday, he added that "we could be looking at another late October buying period."
Election Day is Nov. 3. The S&P 500 has been higher a year after every midterm since 1950, all 19 of them.
The payoff can take a while. In 2018, stocks kept falling after the vote, entered a bear market, and didn't bottom until Christmas Eve. And 19 elections is a small sample, especially in a year when the AI trade that powered the rally is the one cracking.
The next few weeks will tell. If stocks carve out a late-October low and the average stock keeps leading, the midterm playbook is right on schedule. If chips drag the S&P 500 to new lows after Nov. 3, 2026 is writing its own script.
Internal AI tools helped analyze interview transcripts, research, and draft this post. Humans reviewed, edited, and fact-checked this post before publication.

articles.title_orig: DIA Releases Clearest Image of China’s Reusable Spaceplane with Service Module Attached
articles.title_zh: DIA Releases Clearest Image of China’s Reusable Spaceplane with Service Module Attached
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) has released a new image of China’s secretive reusable spaceplane, captured by a Maxar Technologies spacecraft in 2024. Published in the DIA’s “Challenges to Security in Space” report on Oct. 26, 2026, the photo provides a rare view of the spacecraft in orbit with its service module attached.
China’s reusable experimental spacecraft has flown four orbital missions since September 2020, launched aboard Long March 2F rockets. The first mission lasted two days; the second, launched in August 2022, remained in orbit for 276 days; and the third, launched in December 2023, lasted 268 days. A fourth mission began in February 2026.
Before the release of the Maxar image, public imagery was limited to grainy ground-based telescope observations and computer-generated illustrations with Chinese markings. Space tracking forums in early 2023 observed the Chinese spacecraft connecting with another object multiple times, but no image existed at the time.
The Maxar image used in the DIA report is dated to 2024, when the spacecraft launched in December 2023 was still in orbit during its third mission. The timing is therefore consistent with the photograph depicting the vehicle during that flight, although the exact date of capture has not been publicly disclosed.
Behold: The US Defense Intelligence Agency has released a report on challenges to security in space, including an NEI image of China’s spaceplane from Maxar, taken in 2024. https://t.co/F3msSwoFph
— Andrew Jones (@AJ_FI) October 27, 2026
The report identifies two Chinese space models, Shenlong and Tengyun, but it is not known which of those is in the image. The Chinese spacecraft is often compared with the U.S. Space Force’s X-37B because both are uncrewed reusable orbital vehicles designed to return to Earth.
However, the Chinese vehicle’s design, payload, and mission objectives remain largely undisclosed. Tracking data indicate that it has deployed objects and performed rendezvous and proximity operations, but these observations do not establish the spacecraft’s intended military role.
The spaceplane appears in the DIA’s broader assessment of space-related capabilities and threats, whose goal is to cover the capabilities of strategic rivals. “The updated report details the space defense and military goals, including strategies, plans and intentions, of China, Russia and the emerging space powers of Iran and North Korea,” says the press release .
The image provides a view of the underside of China’s reusable spaceplane, with its service module attached and solar arrays deployed. The module is understood to provide electrical power and propulsion during the orbital mission before separating from the spaceplane ahead of reentry, similarly to the X-37B’s service module.
The image also appears to show the spacecraft’s payload-bay doors, although the precise configuration and function of the visible features have not been publicly detailed. Among the possibilities are systems like robotic arms, small satellites or specimens for in-orbit testing.
Now then — this could be something exceptional. The rumours are that inside this exceptional payload fairing atop a CZ-2F is a CASC spaceplane, launching from Jiuquan Friday. Source: 俊了个锅 via 林晓弈。 https://t.co/qs6VRfzQoP https://t.co/ZPnpwAIfyO
— Andrew Jones (@AJ_FI) September 3, 2020
Beijing launched its first ever reusable spaceplane prototype on Sep. 4, 2020 aboard a Long March 2F carrier rocket from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China’s Gobi desert. The spacecraft remained in orbit for two days before returning to Earth.
Although Chinese authorities did not initially disclose the landing site in detail, open-source analysis of satellite imagery associated the landing with a runway near the Lop Nur nuclear test site in northwestern China.
Since its launch on 4 August 2022, we observed multiple large maneuvers raising the object’s altitude — as well as repeated deployments, formation flying, and docking of a sub-satellite Object J (NORAD ID 54218). https://t.co/ORVgSXYKmJ
— LeoLabs (@LeoLabs_Space) May 8, 2023
The second launch of the space plane took place on Aug. 4, 2022, this time spending 276 days in orbit until May 8, 2023. According to the DIA, the vehicle appeared to “maneuver with a companion satellite and conduct station-keeping at around 1 km separation.”
“At one point, the two objects appeared within 100 meters of one another. The spaceplane and satellite possibly rendezvoused before the satellite was re-released,” the DIA report said.
This event tested our object tracking and maneuver detection and characterization capabilities, proving that we can provide critical intelligence on the behaviors and activities of objects in #LEO thanks to our continuous, real-time operations. https://t.co/WDP06ffBSv
— LeoLabs (@LeoLabs_Space) May 8, 2023
On May 8, 2023, commercial space-tracking company LeoLabs reported that its observations indicated repeated deployments, formation flying, and apparent docking or capture operations involving ‘Object J’:
“Since its launch on 4 August 2022, we observed multiple large maneuvers raising the object’s altitude – as well as repeated deployments, formation flying, and docking of a sub-satellite Object J (NORAD ID 54218). We’ve determined that the Test Spacecraft2 has propulsive capability and engaged in proximity operations with Object J, including what appeared to be at least two and possibly three capture/docking operations.”
China launched the spacecraft on its third orbital mission on Dec. 14, 2023. It remained in orbit for 268 days, returning on Sept. 6, 2024, according to the DIA report.
During that flight, the spacecraft again “released and interacted with an object,”according to the DIA. Considering that the Maxar image was captured in 2024, we can presume the vehicle was photographed during this third mission.
Although this was not covered by the report, the spacecraft’s fourth mission began in February 2026. Orbital-tracking data analyzed by astronomer Jonathan McDowell indicated that the vehicle released and subsequently recaptured the same object, whose precise identity and purpose remain unknown, with similar operations reportedly repeated later in the flight.
then executed a rerendezvous with the subsat on Sep 10 and a recapture on Sep  13. This analysis is based on USSF GP data. USSF also cataloged an additional object 24J on about Sep 10, but with no orbit data; I think this was a mistake and is a duplicate of object 24H.
— Jonathan McDowell (@planet4589) September 23, 2026
The spacecraft’s proximity operations have raised questions about potential counterspace applications, with some theories assigning more exotic kinetic ‘anti-satellite’ capabilities to the Chinese spacecraft.
While there is no evidence yet the vehicle is designed as a kinetic anti-satellite weapon, and the spaceplane’s intended mission remains undisclosed, space is becoming a contested domain. The observed rendezvous and capture capabilities can support satellite inspection and servicing, but could also enable interference with other spacecraft.
The spacecraft’s potential military applications remain uncertain. While there is no public evidence confirming that the vehicle carries military payloads, such a platform could be used for space-based reconnaissance, intelligence-gathering, and monitoring of other space objects, as well as kinetic missions possibly involving the use of directed energy weapons, offensive weapons or electronic warfare.
America’s X37B compared to China’s orbital Spaceplane. https://t.co/DPC4W3euTW
— David Willis (@ThePrimalDino) October 27, 2026
China has however maintained a non-military purpose for this spacecraft. A machine translation of a Xinhua report of the Aug. 5, 2022 launch said:

articles.title_orig: Fed meeting live updates: Federal Reserve weighs elevated inflation, midterm elections as October meeting kicks off
articles.title_zh: Fed meeting live updates: Federal Reserve weighs elevated inflation, midterm elections as October meeting kicks off
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The Federal Reserve kicked off its two-day policy meeting on Tuesday as elevated inflation continues to pose a problem for central bankers who nevertheless seem reluctant to hike rates this month.
Fed watchers expect the central bank to keep benchmark rates in the 3.75% to 4% range , with bond traders pricing in a less than 10% chance of a hike on Wednesday, per CME Group. A rate hike in December appears far more likely, however, according to the Fed's dot plot and fed funds futures.
Although recent inflation data came in hotter than expected , several officials' remarks suggest the Fed will hold rates this month to continue assessing additional data. The proximity of the October meeting to the US midterm elections next Tuesday is also seen as a deterrent to bold monetary policy moves.
With the Fed holding rates steady seen as all but given, the focus is on what Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh will say at his post-FOMC-meeting press conference on Wednesday. Warsh has deliberately avoided telegraphing future Fed policy moves, but hot inflation could elicit more insight from him into the path forward.
Federal Reserve interest rate changes on the eve of elections are tricky propositions, but for the third election in a row, the central bank may be unable to dodge that prospect after a hot inflation reading on Wednesday.
New Consumer Price Index data showed inflation heated up again in September , rising 3.7% annually and posting a 0.6% month-over-month surge. Core inflation, the measure more closely watched by the Fed, was also hotter than expected, rising 2.6% annually and 0.3% monthly. Following Wednesday's CPI release, odds of an October rate hike immediately spiked.
That new data comes as the next Federal Open Market Committee interest rate decision is scheduled for Oct. 28, just six days before Election Day.
"There is a political implication for going in October," Wolfe Research chief economist Stephanie Roth told Yahoo Finance on Wednesday, adding that committee members "would very much prefer not to do it," but the data is making a rate hike a distinct possibility.
"This makes the October meeting live," Roth said of the inflation reading.
Markets are heading into a busy few days for global central bank rate announcements.
Five major central banks are scheduled to make policy decisions this week, with two expected to hike and three to hold.
On Wednesday, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand and the Bank of Canada will announce their decisions before the Fed releases its FOMC statement. Both central banks are expected to hike rates.
In Canada's case, the BOC is caught between a weakening economy and higher inflation. Governor Tiff Macklem has signaled in recent months that he is concerned about higher oil prices bleeding through to broader price inflation.
The next day, the European Central Bank is expected to hold rates steady, as is the Bank of Japan on Friday.
Many economists see the overall bias of central banks tilting toward tighter policy next year as artificial intelligence and the war in the Middle East drive inflation higher.
"If you're a central banker ... you've got to recognize this as a shock," Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said about AI at the IMF annual meeting this month.
The major US stock indexes rose on Tuesday as investors anticipated the Fed's decision on Wednesday.
The Dow ( ^DJI ) edged just above the flat line, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) rose 0.6% and the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) gained 1.2% amid a semiconductor stock rally.
The US dollar index ( DX-Y.NYB ) rose above 102, and the 10-year Treasury yield ( ^TNX ) remained steady at 4.99%. Bitcoin ( BTC-USD ) also rose to above $80,600.
Conviction that the Fed would hold rates steady firmed on Tuesday, with traders expecting just 7% odds of a hike. Unless the Fed opts for a surprise hike, the decision is unlikely to move markets much.
But watch what happens to assets when Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh begins speaking tomorrow. Investors will be on alert for any hawkish signals.
The Federal Open Market Committee's two-day policy meeting has started and will conclude at 2 p.m. ET on Wednesday.
The FOMC's decision on whether to cut, hold, or raise interest rates will be released at 2 p.m. tomorrow. Following that decision, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh will hold a news conference at 2:30 p.m. that will be live-streamed.
This is the seventh FOMC meeting this year. The final Fed meeting of the year will take place from Dec. 8-9 and will include a Summary of Economic Projections, which will be used to gauge where policymakers see rates heading in 2027.
The Federal Reserve heads into its interest-rate decision this week facing hotter inflation, keeping the meeting live even as markets widely expect the central bank to hold interest rates steady just days before the midterm elections.
Alan Blinder, a former Fed vice chair and a Princeton University economics professor, is expecting a "hawkish pause."
Although Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh doesn't favor telegraphing the central bank's next move, Blinder said the moment calls for clarity.
"This is a perfect time for clear forward guidance that doesn't quite say, but strongly hints, we're pausing now, but we stand ready to raise again and even give a hint that the next meeting might be the next interest rate hike."
The Federal Reserve's two-day policy meeting kicked off this morning at 9:30 a.m. ET, as scheduled, a Fed spokesperson confirmed.
Expectations remain firm that the Fed will hold rates steady in a range of 3.75% to 4% after hiking by 25 basis points in September. Traders broadly view that the Fed will hike again in December.
But in October, there's a strong belief the Fed won't move rates. According to CME Group's FedWatch, traders see a 90% chance of no move.

articles.title_orig: European Leaders Split Over Phone Call to Putin
articles.title_zh: European Leaders Split Over Phone Call to Putin
articles.content_orig:
The leaders of Finland and Norway have held a joint call with Vladimir Putin - rare contact between the Russian president and European leaders.
Finland's President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said the aim of the call had been to "convey messages directly regarding future negotiations" towards peace. An end to the conflict in Ukraine "will not be achieved through silence," Stubb said.
Neither side suggested the needle had been moved on ending the war, which began when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Although the Finnish leader said the conversation with Putin had been "frank and substantive," Støre added that there were "big differences in views" with Putin.
Several European leaders have recently shown willingness to engage with Russia directly, but both Stubb and Støre pointed out their initiative was taken in their capacity as neighbours of Russia, rather than on behalf of Europe as a whole.
"We've not set out to speak on behalf of anyone other than ourselves," Støre said.
Stubb added the call had been prepared in consultation with Ukraine and the US following a meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, the Nordic leaders and US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo last week.
The first trilateral US-Ukraine-Russia talks since the start of the year are tentatively planned for early November in Abu Dhabi.
Zelensky later confirmed Stubb and Støre debriefed him after the call and said he was grateful for their "active support", while his Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the call had been "the right approach".
Finland and Norway, which border Russia, initiated the 90-minute call - held from Helsinki - to "discuss Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and the diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe", the leaders' offices said.
Støre added: "The war comes with enormous human and material costs... The suffering and destruction will impact generations."
The Kremlin said Putin told the leaders that "a just and lasting peace" would only be possible if Russia's interests were considered.
Putin also reaffirmed to the Nordic leaders what he views as the "root causes" of the conflict - his frequent shorthand for Ukraine's desire to exist as a sovereign state.
"A fair long-term peace settlement is possible only if Russia's legal interests are taken into account fully and unconditionally", Putin said.
All three parties reportedly agreed to continue their direct phone communication.
There was no official EU reaction to the talks. The dialogue had not been coordinated with other European leaders, the Danish and Swedish prime ministers said. "I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo," commented Sweden's Ulf Kristersson.
Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Stubb had informed him that Europe's position on the upcoming talks in the United Arab Emirates was "moderately optimistic".
Relations between the US and Ukraine and its European allies have soured since US President Donald Trump agreed to lift some sanctions from Russia, allowing Moscow to export oil to the America.
As the Trump administration's position on Russia has softened, several European leaders have said Europe should be trying to re-establish direct contacts with the Kremlin.
Stubb and Støre are the first European leaders to contact Putin since French President Emmanuel Macron's conversation with him in July 2025.
Soon after, Putin visited Alaska for a summit with Trump, and from then on Europeans were further sidelined from Ukraine peace talks. Moscow regularly mocks European leaders and accuses the EU of prolonging the war by supplying Ukraine with weapons.
But last weekend, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said having a European negotiator at the peace talks table would be "good".
And although he said Moscow did not view Finland and Norway as speaking on behalf of Europe, on Tuesday Peskov conceded that Stubb and Støre's talks with Putin had been "very constructive and practical talks with the leaders of two key neighbouring states."

articles.title_orig: Researchers are getting tired of OpenAI gatekeeping its breakthroughs
articles.title_zh: Researchers are getting tired of OpenAI gatekeeping its breakthroughs
articles.content_orig:
Expert ‘shepherds’ will decide how best to share the latest breakthroughs in computer science and physics.
Expert ‘shepherds’ will decide how best to share the latest breakthroughs in computer science and physics.
On Monday, OpenAI announced impressive breakthroughs in mathematics, computer science, and physics, along with what the company says is an evolving approach to communicating its findings. But despite its apparent course correction, researchers who spoke to The Verge are growing increasingly tired of the company’s antics.
It has been a turbulent few months between OpenAI and mathematicians, who are still grappling with the hundreds of preprints unceremoniously dumped on them at the start of October. This time, OpenAI says it is working with expert “shepherds” to decide how best to share its latest breakthroughs.
All three results concern some of the most consequential unsolved problems in mathematics, computer science, and physics. Some extend OpenAI’s previous work and others break new ground. Following advice from OpenAI’s “shepherds,” each has a different release strategy. For the mathematics result, OpenAI released the AI-generated output, “leaving researchers free to organize their own efforts to explain the result.” For its computer science finding, OpenAI will also assemble an external group of researchers “to explain the result.” Physics, meanwhile, has not been released at all, and OpenAI said it will “defer” to an external group of experts about how to release the materials.
Given the varying levels of disclosure and the complexity of evaluating such work, it is difficult for researchers to fully judge the company’s findings. Even with all of the information, doing so would take time. But experts who spoke to The Verge said there are good reasons to take the results seriously, variously describing them as “huge,” “major breakthroughs,” and “significant.”
“It doesn’t make any sense that first only a few distinguished scientists can look at them.”
But researchers’ excitement about the science was tempered by exasperation with OpenAI’s conduct, a familiar feeling after months of what they describe as an exhausting barrage of AI-generated findings. Many were eager for the wider community to get on with the arduous task of scrutinizing the AI lab’s findings and questioned why OpenAI was putting up additional barriers by handpicking experts to oversee the process.
Most experts The Verge spoke to welcomed OpenAI’s decision to consult outside researchers, but argued that publicly announcing results should also mean making that work available for anyone to scrutinize. “I am fine with them releasing the problems as they did today,” said Constantin Kogler, a researcher at the Institute for Advanced Study, welcoming the more manageable batch of three results compared with the hundreds released previously. But he questioned the decision to restrict access to experts of OpenAI’s choosing. “It doesn’t make any sense that first only a few distinguished scientists can look at them,” he said.
“The fact that they handpick the group is a disaster,” Andreas Karch, a physics professor at the University of Texas at Austin, told The Verge . “The large labs have enough power as it is. They should not be picking winners and losers.” Karch initially suggested selecting researchers through a “competitive process,” though he acknowledged it would likely produce a similar group, which he described as “first rate.” Later, he questioned why OpenAI “can’t release the proof now,” in addition to appointing its team of experts. “This would democratize access while still showing that they care about making the results meaningful and understandable,” he said.
“My sense is that for any approach, there is going to be someone who is upset.”
It is exactly the kind of gatekeeping the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI), a group of experts OpenAI had previously pledged to consult on how to share its findings, warned against just a day before the announcement. “We recommend that AI companies do not adopt this practice,” they said, arguing that selecting certain people to receive the output first is “unnecessary,” borrows the reputation of selected researchers, and risks unequal access, biased selection, and delays, among other issues. Instead, they recommended that AI labs release output on scholarly repositories, with formalized proofs and information on how the problems were chosen, and provide funding and other support for people working on understanding the results.
Following the publication of the latest results, AGMAI urged OpenAI to “make public without delay the natural-language and Lean outputs behind its announced” results in physics:
”While these are central questions in physics, they are also important questions in mathematics. The existence of quantum Yang–Mills theory is part of a Millennium Prize problem and the construction of interacting quantum field theories in four dimensions has been a goal of mathematical physics for decades.
We have great respect for the scientists asked by OpenAI to lead this work. But as we explained in our recent statement , understanding should develop in the open, with everyone given the same access. OpenAI have said they delayed release until the Lean formalization was complete. By their own account this is now complete, so there is no scientific reason for delaying the release any further.”
Making the findings openly available could also lead to better science and encourage wider adoption of new tools like AI, Hassett said. “Having many groups around the world wrestle with these results supports rapid adoption of new tools by those that would like to use them,” he said.
”Fundamental results are being solved so quickly without human contribution ... the papers are difficult to read and verify.”
Finding a way to communicate with researchers in the fields OpenAI is increasingly encroaching on that satisfies everyone may be impossible. The company says it is experimenting with different approaches and acknowledges that each has tradeoffs. “My sense is that for any approach, there is going to be someone who is upset,” said Stanford mathematician Jared Duker Lichtman. “So it’s just a question of finding the least offensive option.”
Xiaoyu He, a mathematics professor at the Georgia Institute of Technology, thinks the problem is deeper than how OpenAI chooses to announce its findings. ”The results are very impressive,” he said, “but I think they are making a show of trying to be responsible and thoughtful about how they release results while not being able to change the main issues: that fundamental results are being solved so quickly without human contribution, and that the papers are difficult to read and verify.”

United Parcel Service on Tuesday reported third-quarter results that beat Wall Street expectations and raised its full-year guidance.
The guidance raise comes after the company already upped its outlook last quarter . UPS now said it's projecting full-year consolidated revenue of approximately $92.6 billion, up from its previous expectations of $91.2 billion, as well as fourth-quarter revenue of $25.7 billion.
Shares of UPS rose slightly in morning trading.
Here's how the company performed in its third quarter, compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
For the quarter ended Sept. 30, UPS reported net income of $1.16 billion, or $1.37 per share, down slightly from net income of $1.31 billion, or $1.55, the year prior. Adjusting for one-time expenses, UPS reported earnings per share of $1.69. Revenue rose 6.7% to $22.9 billion.
In its domestic segment, the company said it saw a 4.5% increase in revenue, while its international segment had a 7.1% rise in revenue. Its supply chain solutions business saw an 18.2% revenue increase, which UPS said was primarily driven to growth in forwarding and logistics, including healthcare . On a call with analysts, CEO Carol Tomé said healthcare revenue exceeded $3 billion for the third consecutive quarter.
The company had previously said it expected its third-quarter domestic revenue to be flat and for domestic average daily volume to fall due to seasonal declines and the glide down with Amazon .
"We're driving more premium growth, improving revenue quality and mix, and creating greater operating leverage through a more efficient network," Tomé said on the call. "All of this is strengthening the underlying performance of our business."
UPS has been in the midst of a turnaround under Tomé's leadership, working to create a leaner business model and leveraging automation to position the company for growth.
As the company prepares for its peak holiday season, Tomé said the consumer remains resilient, and the growth in average daily volume between the third and fourth quarters will be consistent with last year. However, fourth-quarter domestic average daily volume is expected to fall due to the reduction with Amazon.
She added that nearly 70% of all packages will flow through an automated process this holiday season.

articles.title_orig: Robinhood Misses Q3 Earnings as Crypto Revenue Rises and Prediction Market Bets Grow
articles.title_zh: Robinhood Misses Q3 Earnings as Crypto Revenue Rises and Prediction Market Bets Grow
articles.content_orig:
Robinhood, the trading app where more than 28 million people keep money to buy stocks and crypto and now bet on sports and elections, reported third-quarter revenue of $1.42 billion billion on Tuesday, missing the roughly $1.43 billion Wall Street expected
Earnings came in at $0.51 per share, missing the $0.55 analysts projected and down from $0.61 a year ago. Earnings per share is profit divided by the number of shares outstanding, and it is the figure investors use to call a quarter a beat or a miss.
Robinhood is the app that brought commission-free trading to a generation of first-time investors, which makes its quarterly report one of the clearest readings of what ordinary people are doing with their money. When customers trade more, deposit more or pile into new products, the shift shows up in these numbers.
Net income was $476 million, down 14% from $556 million a year earlier and 17% from $573 million in the second quarter. The quarter included a $67 million unrealized loss, meaning a drop in value on paper, on Robinhood Ventures Fund I, which cost $0.07 per share. Adjusted earnings per share, which exclude certain items, came to $0.60, down 3% from a year ago.
Event contracts, the yes-or-no bets that pay out $1 if a game, an election or an economic report goes a certain way, brought in $173 million, up from $156 million in the second quarter, when they overtook crypto revenue for the first time. Customers traded a record 16.4 billion of them, more than seven times a year earlier.
“I believe we’re at the very beginning of a prediction market supercycle,” CEO Vlad Tenev said in December last year, when Robinhood added NFL player contracts and parlay-style combos that pay only if every outcome hits.
Crypto trading revenue rose to $120 million from $100 million in the second quarter, but remained down 55% from the $268 million Robinhood earned in the third quarter of 2025. Customers traded $50 billion in crypto during the quarter, down 38% from a year earlier, with $21 billion on the Robinhood app and $29 billion through Bitstamp, the crypto exchange it acquired
Robinhood Chain went live on July 1 as a layer-2 network, meaning a blockchain that runs on top of Ethereum to make transactions cheaper and faster. Its first weeks were driven by meme coins , joke-themed tokens, rather than the tokenized stocks it was built for, which are digital versions of company shares that trade on a blockchain.
By the end of August the chain had earned about $3.13 million in fees over 30 days, more than Ethereum and Base , which came in at $2.47 million and $2.89 million.
Hours before the report, Robinhood announced a deal with Ripple that brings RLUSD, a stablecoin (a crypto token designed to stay worth one dollar), to Robinhood Chain and Bitstamp, with an in-app rollout planned later this year. RLUSD has a market value above $2.5 billion, and Ripple will also supply Robinhood’s treasury software and lending for Bitstamp traders.
Robinhood shares closed Tuesday at about $94.61 and slipped in after-hours trading- The stock is down roughly 18% this year and about 37% below its 52-week high of $150.47.
Robinhood narrowed its 2026 outlook for adjusted operating expenses and stock-based pay to $2.675 billion to $2.75 billion, trimming the top of the $2.675 billion to $2.775 billion range it set in July.

articles.title_orig: Overseas Handler Linked to Iran Behind Foiled RAF Air Base Attack
articles.title_zh: Overseas Handler Linked to Iran Behind Foiled RAF Air Base Attack
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — Two men were charged under the National Security Act on Tuesday over an incident last month at the RAF Fairford airbase , with prosecutors accusing a British national of trying to help Iranian intelligence in Britain.
RAF Fairford had been used by U.S. bombers to carry out strikes on Iran, but they were withdrawn on security grounds shortly after five British men were arrested outside the base in southwest England early Sept. 27.
The circumstances of the incident, which remain largely unexplained, attracted huge international attention, coming at a time of heightened concern about the security implications for Western states of the war between the United States and Iran.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said this month that the activity at RAF Fairford was likely to have been coordinated in Iran, which Tehran’s ambassador to Britain has denied.
British national Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, was charged with engaging in conduct that was likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service between Aug. 31 and Sept. 28, with police saying the country is believed to be Iran.
Nouman Essghir, a 24-year-old dual British-Iranian national who was first arrested outside RAF Fairford on Sept. 27, was charged with one offense of entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the U.K. on Aug. 22.
The pair will appear at London’s Westminster Magistrates’ Court later on Tuesday.
Police said that six other people, four of whom are British nationals who were arrested outside RAF Fairford on Sept. 27, remain on police bail.
The decision to bail suspects after an apparent major incident had drawn scrutiny, but on Tuesday police said that decision had helped secure charges against the two men.
“We know the decisions made during our investigations can sometimes appear illogical to those on the outside, but I want to make it very clear that there will always be a good reason or rationale behind them,” said Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing in the U.K.
“In this case, this decision-making has led to swifter progress, better evidence and ultimately us securing the charges that I have announced today.”

articles.title_orig: Apple’s low-cost iPhone 18 details revealed by leaker
articles.title_zh: Apple’s low-cost iPhone 18 details revealed by leaker
articles.content_orig:
Apple 's most affordable iPhone is getting some neat new features, but a 120Hz display isn't one of them.
This is according to leaker Digital Chat Station, who shared his findings on Weibo .
According to the report, the iPhone 18e will have a 60Hz, 6.12-inch OLED display, Apple's new A20 chip, a single, 48-megapixel camera, and a 24-megapixel front camera.
That last one sounds a bit unlikely, as even the latest iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max only have an 18-megapixel selfie camera. Apple doesn't typically bestow top features on its most affordable device.
The A20 chip sounds more likely; the iPhone "e" series traditionally had a powerful chip, with the company cutting costs on cameras and displays.
Speaking of display, the 60Hz refresh rate is a bit disappointing, but it also seems pretty likely, given that the new iPad mini , which launched earlier this week, features a 60Hz OLED display.
The iPhone 18e is likely to launch in spring 2027, alongside the iPhone 18 and Apple's super-thin iPhone Air 2.

articles.title_orig: Code-execution flaw in UEFI firmware affects most servers on planet Earth
articles.title_zh: Code-execution flaw in UEFI firmware affects most servers on planet Earth
articles.content_orig:
Defenders across the world face the burden of responding to yet another botched code-execution vulnerability, this time in boot-time firmware used by most of the world’s server vendors and data centers.
The vulnerability, with a severity rating of 9.5 out of 10, resides in the TianoCore EDK II , an open source codebase that hardware makers and cloud providers use to create the UEFI firmware that runs during the boot-up sequence. Last year, a representative of the UEFI Forum called EDK2 the “preeminent solution / implementation of the UEFI specifications.” Virtually all UEFI suppliers (sometimes still called IBVs or independent BIOS vendors), including AMI, Insyde, and Phoenix, use the reference code extensively. Project Mu, Microsoft’s hardened EDK2 fork, used the code containing the vulnerable component as well.
The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, is a memory-corruption flaw in an ICMP component that attackers can exploit to execute malicious code that runs before the operating system and firmware can implement defenses like Secure Boot , which establishes a chain of trust for all code, including the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), loaded during boot. While final payloads delivered by CVE-2026-97631 have no persistence—meaning they run only once—they can give attackers a wide opening to install other payloads that also run each time early in the boot process.
The parties that discovered CVE-2026-97631—Alex Matrosov of Anthropic and Dan Holmes of Google—had arranged for it to stay under wraps until a coordinated disclosure that was scheduled for January. AMI, a maker of motherboards and other hardware, published this pull request last month that detailed the vulnerability and included a code fix. Once the post came to the attention of the discovering parties, TianoCore Project members published a public advisory last week.
With publicly available patch code, it will be trivial for advanced hackers to learn how the vulnerability is triggered and to build working exploits. Further compounding the urgency, patching UEFI code vulnerabilities in millions of end devices sold and used by thousands of hardware makers and cloud providers is cumbersome and time-consuming. Word of the vulnerability comes six days after another botched disclosure, this one involving a critical code-execution vulnerability in the PHP programming language.
“This vulnerability in the ICMP parser of the EDK2 network stack is interesting in terms of how it affects the chain of trust and the broader ecosystem,” said HD Moore, creator of Metasploit and chief research officer at security firm Dragos. “An attacker intent on compromising a nearby endpoint or server could use this bug to hijack program flow at a point where the boot process still has access to sensitive components, like the endpoint’s TPM. This could be used to break disk encryption for cases where an attacker has short-term network access (and it would be even easier in a theft scenario).”
CVE-2026-97631 is a 16-year-old buffer overflow in the PXE-Base Code driver (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe), which is responsible for allowing servers, storage equipment, and other devices to boot using code downloaded from a local network. During this process—known as the pre-execution environment boot—the driver uses a network listener to monitor for ICMP errors. Because the driver doesn’t enforce a memory copy limit of 504 bytes, overwriting adjacent data, a malicious insider or a hacker who has gained low-level access to a local network can send an error message that appends code past this limit. The IUEFI module running on the CPU then becomes corrupted.
As the official advisory puts it:
During network boot, the PXE Base Code driver (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe) keeps a receive request open for ICMP error messages and copies each received message into the fixed 504-byte field Mode.IcmpError of its private context structure. The copy loop’s bounds handling is incorrect in both the IPv4 and IPv6 handlers (PxeBcIcmpErrorDpcHandle and PxeBcIcmp6ErrorDpcHandle): for a message longer than 504 bytes it still copies bytes into the field, and it advances the destination pointer by the cumulative rather than the per-fragment length, so an oversized message writes attacker-controlled bytes past the field. Nothing earlier on the receive path restricts the message length.
The malicious error can be delivered through a simple unicast sent from any network distance to a target device’s IP address, as long as it’s sent during the PXE boot sequence. An attacker can deliver a denial-of-service by causing the boot sequence to hang. When the attacker knows what the target firmware build is, it can plant a “counterfeit event” that executes the malicious code on the CPU in its UEFI firmware environment. The code runs in ring 0, a CPU’s most privileged execution level. Because exploits bypass attestation processes designed to cryptographically prove to remote servers that the hardware is secure, they present a key opportunity for elevating limited privileges.
CVE-2026-97631 joins a long list of previously discovered vulnerabilities in UEFI or code that works closely with it. The most severe of them, LogoFail , stemmed from logo images included in the UEFI of just about every hardware maker. Rendering bugs allowed attackers to subvert the chain of trust UEFI enforces and go on to install malicious components before the OS loaded or Secure Boot ran. PixieFail was a vulnerability similar to CVE-2026-97631. It, too, was the result of faulty PXE boot flaws in EDK2. Following discovery of the vulnerability, researchers embarked on multiple fuzzing projects designed to surface other critical flaws in the open source code library. It appears those efforts failed to find this latest flaw.
Other recently discovered UEFI flaws include:
Like CVE-2026-97631, exploitation or use of these payloads is appealing because it allows attackers to infect machines early in the boot process, before TPM and other defenses load, so they can inflict maximum damage. Given the ubiquity of CVE-2026-97631, Moore said it’s likely a “forever” bug that will live on in end-of-support systems.
There are important caveats and limitations to exploiting this latest vulnerability. As noted, some level of control over a local network is a prerequisite. That likely limits exploitation to insiders or attackers, such as nation-states or ransomware operators, who manage to gain low-level access inside a network and are looking for a way to elevate system rights. There’s no evidence yet that CVE-2026-97631 provides an initial entry point into a network. There are other hurdles to clear.
“For exploiting the vulnerability itself, an attacker needs to guess specific addresses within the target system, so it’s not something that you can throw a single exploit at any target and get RCE across a diverse range of devices, but it needs to be tuned for each target model/version/configuration since the addresses will change based on those,” Jesse Michael, a principal researcher at firmware security firm Eclypsium, told Ars. “Unlike some of the previous, high-profile vulnerabilities like BootHole, Black Lotus, and Baton Drop, this vulnerability can be fixed with a basic code fix, which will require deploying a BIOS/UEFI update, but they don’t need to deal with revocations, pk/kek/db/dbx key management updates, or making sure to update OS and provisioning media like you do with Secure Boot bypasses in the bootloader itself.”
CVE-2026-97631 doesn’t affect home and small office users, or any other users who boot their devices solely from disk drives. Instead, it applies only to organizations with machines that boot from local networks, or conceivably from Internet-connected resources. Even then, the targeted firmware must rely on EDK2, as opposed to a different reference implementation, and use the PXE functionality (which is turned on by default).

articles.title_orig: Butter Recalled for Yeast, Mold, and E. Coli Contamination—Here’s What to Know
articles.title_zh: Butter Recalled for Yeast, Mold, and E. Coli Contamination—Here’s What to Know
articles.content_orig:
Design elements: Getty Images. EatingWell design.
Plant-based butter is being recalled right now due to yeast, mold and E. coli contamination, according to the U.S. Food & Drug Administration.
Just over 1,300 cases of Miyoko’s Creamery European Style Salted Plant Milk Butter have been voluntarily recalled and pulled from retail shelves in Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Maryland, New Jersey, New Hampshire and Wisconsin.
If you think you might have the recalled product on hand, check the box for a lot code of 07871 and a best-by date of November 11, 2026. This recall has been deemed a Class II recall by the FDA, meaning that consuming the butter may lead to “temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences or where the probability of serious adverse health consequences is remote.”
If you have this product in your fridge or freezer, do not consume it. E. coli can cause symptoms like diarrhea, stomach cramps, nausea, vomiting and fever. Consuming a food product with high levels of yeast and/or mold can also cause symptoms of illness. If you are experiencing any adverse effects after consuming this product, make sure to contact a health care professional.
If you have any questions about this ongoing recall, contact the FDA at 1-888-INFO-FDA (1-888-463-6332).

articles.content_orig:
Robinhood shares fell 4% in after-hours trading as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.
Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30,  compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.
Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting the focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.
Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.
Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.
Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.
Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.
Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

articles.title_orig: 4 Powerful Android Tablets To Buy Instead Of The New OLED iPad Mini
articles.title_zh: 4 Powerful Android Tablets To Buy Instead Of The New OLED iPad Mini
articles.content_orig:
Ahead of its 'Pro and Tell' event, the company has already launched a few new devices.
Apple wasn't done with its product reveals for the fall after unveiling the iPhone Duo , iPhone 18 Pro models and an array of smart home devices . Nor could it wait until the third event of the season, dubbed "Pro and Tell," to show off more gear.
The company got a string of announcements underway on Monday with the reveal of the long-awaited OLED iPad mini. Tuesday brought us an M6-powered iMac and 14-inch MacBook Pro. It's expected that Apple will unveil a touchscreen MacBook as well.
Elsewhere, Apple released the latest versions of its operating systems. Among other things, those added more Siri AI features and made the assistant available in more languages. The company updated Apple Creator Studio with more AI features and creative tools as well.
We'll update this story if and when Apple makes more announcements. In the meantime, here's everything Apple has announced so far this week.
It feels like we've been waiting for forever for Apple to put an OLED display in the iPad mini but that day has finally arrived. The new display has double the peak brightness of the one on the previous model at 1,200 nits, and it has a 2,000,000:1 contrast ratio. The base storage remains the same at 128GB, though if you opt for 256GB or 512GB of storage, you can snag a variant with a nano-texture glass display. That'll cost you extra, naturally.
The company managed to squeeze in a larger screen — an 8.5-inch display rather than the 8.3-inch one in the previous model — without increasing the size of the tablet. In fact, the new iPad mini is slightly narrower than the last one, at 5.22 inches vs. 5.3 inches. It's lighter as well, with the Wi-Fi model coming in at 0.56 pounds (compared with 0.65 pounds last time) and the 5G variant weighing 0.58 pounds (versus 0.66 pounds). The latter, by the way, now boasts Apple's C2 modem, which is said to deliver up to 50 percent faster data speeds than the previous iPad mini. There's also Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread connectivity thanks to the N1 chip.
The OLED iPad mini — the eighth generation of the device — runs on the A20 Pro, the same chipset as the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. Apple says the SoC is capable of running large language models locally, in case you're into that kind of thing. Otherwise, the tablet should be notably faster than earlier models. It supports Apple Intelligence and Siri AI as well, of course. The chipset also boasts a 7-core GPU — two more cores than the A17 Pro, which powered the last-gen iPad mini.
On the camera front, there's a 12MP Center Stage lens on front of the tablet, which Apple has finally shifted to the landscape edge on the iPad mini. However, there's still no Face ID. The 12MP camera on the rear supports 4K 60fps video capture and Smart HDR 4.
The 8th-gen iPad mini has a sealed enclosure to help protect it from the elements. The tablet has an IP67 rating, meaning that it should withstand dust and being immersed in a meter of freshwater for up to 30 minutes, though I would advise against intentionally submerging your iPad mini.
As for battery life, Apple says that should be roughly the same as last time. The company says the new iPad mini should run for up to 10 hours when you're watching video or surfing the web over Wi-Fi. That drops down to nine hours if you're browsing over a cellular connection. If you have at least a 35W power adaptor, you'll be able to recharge the battery to 50 percent of its capacity in 30 minutes, Apple says.
The most interesting thing to me about this iPad mini is that it has Apple's first Acoustic Display, which the company says helps it deliver "an even better audio experience." It claims the tablet offers more volume and "punchier bass" thanks to woofers that "are paired through the display." Apple added that "custom tweeters are now hidden between the glass and aluminum enclosure for clearer highs." I'm definitely curious to find out how all of that sounds in practice.
Inevitably, the latest iPad mini comes with a price hike. It starts at $699, which is $150 more than the previous model after Apple increased the price of that in June . Pre-orders open on October 28, and the tablet will hit shelves on November 6.
On Tuesday, Apple gave the iMac and MacBook Pro spec bumps. The desktop and laptop now each have the M6 chipset , which recently debuted in the Mac mini .
Let's start with the new iMac . Apple says the M6's dual 16-core neural engine enables it to deliver up to five times faster on-device AI performance (for Siri AI, Apple Intelligence and local LLMs) than the previous-gen iMac from 2024 , which had the M4 chipset. The M6 is said to deliver up to 1.5 times faster performance than the M4 for daily tasks, up to two times faster graphics performance (for photo editing etc.) and up to two times higher gaming performance with ray tracing.
The base-level M6 has 10 CPU cores (two super, three performance and two efficiency cores) and a 10-core CPU, compared with eight of each in the M4. There's the option to have a 12-core M6, in which case your desktop will have four Thunderbolt 4 ports instead of the two that the base model has. The four-port model has a nano-texture glass option as well.
Elsewhere, Apple has introduced its N1 networking chip to the iMac. As such, the computer has support for Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread connectivity. It also has the option to add a 2.5Gb Ethernet port, an upgrade from gigabit Ethernet on the M4 iMac.
Specs otherwise are the same as last time. You'll still get a 24-inch 4.5K Super Retina display, a 12MP Center Stage camera, a six‑speaker Dolby Atmos system, at least 16GB of RAM and 256GB of base storage. The dimensions are identical too, though the M6 iMac is a touch lighter than the previous gen at 9.7 pounds (versus 9.74 pounds). Don't expect any changes to the color options either — the new iMac is still available in blue, green, pink, yellow, purple, orange and silver.
One other thing that's staying the same? The starting price, at least after the $200 increase that Apple gave the M4 iMac over the summer. The new model starts at $1,499, and the four-port version will run you at least $1,699. Pre-orders open October 28 and you'll be able to pick one up in store on November 6.
The latest 14-inch MacBook Pro has the 12-core version of the M6 chipset and the N1 networking chip for Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread support. Those appear to be the only spec changes this time.
Compared with the previous-gen 14-inch MBP, which had an M5 SoC, Apple says the M6 model offers up to 30 percent faster graphics performance and up to 25 percent faster AI workloads. It's said to deliver up to 1.3 faster rendering performance with ray tracing in Blender, up to 1.2 times faster image-processing performance in Affinity and up to 1.3 faster project build performance for compiling code in Xcode.
It doesn't seem like this will be a massive upgrade for folks with an M5 model. However, if you have an older MacBook Pro (or really need those incremental improvements from the previous gen), it might be worth making the switch.
Either way, creatives might want to take note of all the updates that are rolling out for Apple Creative Studio . Apple has given Final Cut Pro a long-awaited quality-of-life upgrade by letting you pull clips from the primary storyline and place them anywhere on the timeline, which seems like very basic functionality to have! MotionVFX is integrated into the app on Mac as well, so you'll have thousands of elements at your fingertips for your video edits.
If you have a Mac that supports Apple Intelligence and is set to US English, Logic Pro has an "intelligent assistant" powered by OpenAI that's available in beta. The app has an an enhanced Stem Splitter that can now separate drums as well. In addition, Keynote, Pages and Numbers now have a chatbot you can use to adjust presentations, documents and spreadsheets.
