articles.title_orig: Boeing Stock Plunges After Earnings. 737 Progress Isn’t Fast Enough.
articles.title_zh: Boeing Stock Plunges After Earnings. 737 Progress Isn’t Fast Enough.
articles.content_orig:
Boeing doesn't expect to significantly ramp up output of its best-selling 737 Max aircraft until the second half of 2027 as it grapples with a slower-than-expected pace of wing production.
CEO Kelly Ortberg said Tuesday on the company's quarterly earnings call that Boeing is targeting a production rate of 52 planes a month in the second half of 2027. It has been manufacturing about 47 of its 737 Max planes a month.
Ortberg had told investors last month that the production stabilize was taking a "little bit longer" than expected because of the wings production pace.
Boeing stock fell 10% in trading Tuesday.
"I know everybody wants us to go faster, but we're going to do it right," Ortberg told CNBC's Phil LeBeau in an interview Tuesday.
Ortberg reiterated the company's priority in stabilizing production on Tuesday.
"Looking ahead, expectations are rising, and they should," Ortberg said in a note to staff on Tuesday. "That means elevating our performance through lean, productivity and efficiency improvements in our day-to-day work while upholding our high levels of safety and quality."
Aircraft production and deliveries are key to Boeing's recovery since the bulk of an aircraft's price is paid when the customer receives it.
The company also reported Tuesday that it narrowed its losses in the third quarter, thanks to a boost from its defense unit.
For the three months ended Sept. 30, Boeing reported a net loss of $116 million, or 26 cents a share, compared with a $5.34 billion loss, or $7.14 per share, a year earlier. Adjusting for one-time items, the company posted a loss of 34 cents a share. A year earlier, Boeing had taken a nearly $5 billion charge on its long-delayed 777X aircraft program.
Revenue climbed 4% on the year to $24.19 billion. Free cash flow rose to $464 million from $238 million in the third quarter of 2025.
The company's defense unit revenue jumped 15% in the third quarter from a year earlier to $7.94 billion.
Here's what Boeing reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street analysts expected, according to consensus estimates from LSEG:
Boeing delivered 161 commercial airplanes in the third quarter, one more jet than a year earlier.
Revenue in the all-important commercial aircraft business fell 3% to $10.72 billion. The unit had a negative operating margin of 6.5% because of a "less favorable delivery mix, higher projected costs associated with future production rate adjustments and higher estimated supply chain costs," Boeing said.
Ortberg told staff in a memo that the manufacturer has "more work to do."
The manufacturer had some wins lately. The U.S. Navy tapped Boeing to develop its next-generation fighter jet.
And the Federal Aviation Administration last week signed off on the 737 Max 10 , the largest in the Max family. That followed the approval of the 737 Max 7 in August and marked the final certifications for the aircraft line.

articles.title_zh: Cheerios introduces a Ziploc-sealed cereal bag. Finally.
articles.content_orig:
The No. 1 cereal brand* and the No. 1 most trusted food storage brand** bring freshness you can reseal to the cereal aisle – available exclusively at Walmart.com beginning Oct. 27.
MINNEAPOLIS and RACINE, Wis. — Oct. 27, 2026 — You asked, Cheerios™ and Ziploc® Brand delivered – freshness you can reseal! After receiving hundreds of thousands of requests, comments and reactions annually on the topic, Cheerios and Ziploc® Brand have come together to introduce Cheerios with Ziploc PantrySeal™. The new innovation features the first resealable bag inside a traditional cereal box, making it easier to pour, reseal and help keep cereal fresher longer.
The partnership brings together Cheerios, the No. 1 cereal brand*, with more than 50 years of Ziploc® Brand expertise helping people seal in freshness and store the foods they love. It’s a natural pairing for cereal lovers, 90% of whom say they already take extra steps beyond simply closing the cereal box to help preserve freshness*** like folding the bag, rolling it, clipping it or even transferring it to another container.
“General Mills has received letters, emails and DMs asking for an easier way to reseal a cereal box, and we decided it was time to partner with the ultimate freshness brand: Ziploc®,” said Emilie Knox, Vice President and Business Unit Director for Cheerios at General Mills. “Cheerios with Ziploc PantrySeal™ takes a small, everyday cereal frustration and finally gives consumers the simple solution they’ve been asking for, making the whole routine easier and more enjoyable.”
Cheerios with Ziploc PantrySeal™ is made for how people want to pour a bowl of cereal, as well as store it. The resealable bag is designed to open only partially across the top to create a convenient “pour spout” as an easier way for the whole family to fill a bowl (or a cup, mug or even little hands). Cheerios with Ziploc PantrySeal™ then seals closed right inside the box for cereal freshness you can reseal.
“For generations, Ziploc® Brand has helped people keep the foods they love fresh through simple, trusted solutions,” said a Ziploc® Brand spokesperson. “Cheerios with Ziploc PantrySeal™ is an exciting new expression of what Ziploc® Brand can do – bringing our resealable freshness expertise directly into the Cheerios package and Ziploc® Brand into the pantry in an entirely new way.”
Available as a new option in the cereal aisle for both Cheerios and Honey Nut Cheerios, Cheerios with Ziploc PantrySeal™ combines the same Cheerios families already reach for with Ziploc® Brand’s expertise in resealable storage, for an easier way to open, pour, reseal – and keep enjoying.
A fix that feels this intuitive was anything but simple. With nearly one box of Cheerios produced every second, the new Cheerios with Ziploc PantrySeal™ had to be developed to work at Cheerios scale while keeping the same familiar cereal flowing to pantries nationwide. For Ziploc® Brand, the partnership builds on a history of resealable storage that began with the introduction of its innovative zipper technology in 1968.
And there’s a fitting full-circle connection: Cheerios with Ziploc PantrySeal™ is being produced exclusively in Buffalo, New York, in the same place where Cheerios was first made in 1941.
Cheerios with Ziploc PantrySeal™ is now available exclusively at Walmart.com and will roll out to retailers nationwide in the coming months.
For more information, visit Cheerios.com or follow @Cheerios on Instagram and TikTok . To learn more about Ziploc® Brand, follow @Ziploc on Instagram and @Ziploctheoriginal on TikTok.

articles.title_orig: 500+ lbs of seafood recalled over ‘life-threatening illness’ risks: Do not eat
articles.title_zh: 500+ lbs of seafood recalled over ‘life-threatening illness’ risks: Do not eat
articles.content_orig:
How to Live Better, Longer
Federal regulators are telling consumers in New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, and Pennsylvania not to eat any cold-smoked sprats sold by Haifa Smoked Fish after the Queens company declined the FDA's request to recall them. The agency issued its public advisory on Oct. 23, warning that the small smoked fish were made without required safeguards against Clostridium botulinum , the bacterium that causes botulism.
An FDA inspection of D&M Smoked Fish Inc., which does business as Haifa Smoked Fish, Inc., in Jamaica, Queens, found the firm was producing cold smoked sprats without the controls needed to prevent the bacterium from growing and forming toxin. The FDA recommended a recall of all cold smoked sprats on the market. The firm declined, so the agency issued its own warning.
No illnesses had been reported in the advisory, but the warning covers every lot, and the fish may already be sitting in home freezers, deli cases, and restaurant kitchens, with or without a label.
Several features make this alert harder to act on than a typical grocery recall . The sprats were shipped refrigerated in bulk cardboard boxes and may have been sold at restaurants and grocery store seafood counters with or without a label. The FDA notes that the product may be frozen for up to one year, so fish bought months ago could still be in a household freezer.
Shipping boxes pictured by the FDA carry the Haifa Smoked Fish name and the address 94-15 150 St., Jamaica, N.Y. 11435. For loose fish bought by weight, the agency's guidance is simple: if you cannot tell whether your sprats came from Haifa Smoked Fish, do not eat them and throw them away, or contact the store or supplier.
The FDA also advises anyone who bought or received the product to carefully clean and sanitize surfaces and containers it touched, following its safe food handling guidance .
Without a recall, there is no company-run effort to pull product from stores or contact customers, so food businesses must act on the warning themselves. Federal food safety law allows the FDA to order a mandatory recall in certain cases, but the agency has not announced such a step. It said it will update the alert as new information becomes available.
This is not the first time the company's sprats have raised botulism concerns. In March 2011, D&M Smoked Fish recalled cold smoked sprats and Haifa brand schmaltz herring after New York State Agriculture and Markets sampling found the fish had not been properly eviscerated, a known botulism risk. The recalled sprats went to retailers in Brooklyn.
Botulism toxin attacks the nerves. The FDA lists nausea, vomiting, fatigue or weakness, blurred or double vision, difficulty speaking or a change in voice, trouble swallowing, dry mouth, constipation, and breathing trouble among the symptoms. Paralysis typically moves downward, starting in the face. Drooping eyelids and slurred speech are also common, according to Food Safety News .
Symptoms of foodborne botulism generally begin 18 to 36 hours after eating contaminated food but can appear as soon as six hours or as late as 10 days afterward, the outlet reported. That delay matters. Someone who ate sprats at a weekend family meal might not connect midweek double vision to the food.
Contaminated fish may give no warning. The FDA says food carrying Clostridium botulinum toxin "can look, taste or smell normal, but still make you sick."
The agency is blunt: botulism is a medical emergency, and in severe cases people will die without intensive care. Anyone with these symptoms after eating smoked fish should seek immediate care and tell clinicians what they ate. More background is available from the CDC's botulism page .
The households most likely to be affected are those that buy smoked fish by the pound at seafood and deli counters in the New York metro area and nearby states. The Lakewood Scoop reported that Haifa describes its products as under Orthodox Union kosher supervision, making the warning especially relevant for kosher shoppers.
Distribution was confirmed in Connecticut, New Jersey, New York, and Pennsylvania, but the FDA says the fish may have reached other states. Retailers, restaurants, wholesalers, and food service customers are told not to sell or serve the product.
Families planning gatherings where smoked fish platters are served should check the source before putting sprats on the table.
Illnesses or complaints can be reported through the FDA's consumer assistance page . MedicalDaily will follow any FDA updates, additional states, or changes in the company's position.
What did the FDA warn about? All cold-smoked sprats sold by D&M Smoked Fish Inc., doing business as Haifa Smoked Fish, Inc., of Jamaica, Queens, because they were made without required controls against botulism.
Why is there no recall? The FDA recommended that the company recall the product, but the firm declined. The agency then issued a public warning.
Where were the sprats sold? To retailers, restaurants, wholesalers, and food service customers in Connecticut, New Jersey, New York, and Pennsylvania, and possibly other states.
Have people gotten sick? No illnesses were reported in the FDA's Oct. 23 advisory.
What symptoms should I watch for? Blurred or double vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech, trouble swallowing, weakness, and difficulty breathing. Seek emergency care right away if they appear.
What if my sprats have no label? Do not eat them. Throw them away or ask the store where you bought them, then clean any surfaces or containers they touched.
Can looking at or smelling the fish tell me if it is safe? No. The FDA says contaminated food can look, taste, and smell normal.
Published by Medicaldaily.com

articles.title_orig: AI debt fears ease ahead of Oracle, Alphabet and Amazon updates. Here's what to watch.
articles.title_zh: AI debt fears ease ahead of Oracle, Alphabet and Amazon updates. Here's what to watch.
articles.content_orig:
Fears over artificial intelligence debt have eased after a bout of volatility. But more tests for AI debt are coming.
Oracle holds its Investor Day on Wednesday. And hyperscalers Alphabet and Amazon.com are scheduled to report quarterly results after the market close on Wednesday and Thursday, respectively.
Credit markets are on edge over a flood of AI debt, though fears have eased up a little lately. Meta Platforms ' plans for a $95 billion stock offering , announced on Monday, helped bring down its credit-default swap spreads. Those spreads had risen last week when the company reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter. Other CDS spreads had moved higher too, though they have since backed off.
Investors had expected Meta to bring a large bond deal to market shortly after its earnings announcement, said Richard Cheng, head of Nuveen's investment-grade corporate sector team. The fact that it wasn't announced came as a relief.
"Just the absence of the bond deal itself is a direct catalyst for AI-related spread tightening," he said.
A credit spread is the difference in the yield between the corporate bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. When spreads tighten, it means investors are becoming more confident about the bond issuer.
The market action over the last few days shows that investors are recognizing that "credit fears may have been overblown," said CNBC contributor Paul Meeks, head of technology research at Freedom Capital Markets.
"I expect that these better feelings, maybe not good but better, may continue as companies announce their quarters over the next few weeks."
Still, spreads on CDS remain wider over the past year due to a surge of debt issuance and free cash flows turning negative across the AI space. Meta's CDS spread, for instance, is still up 177% year to date, while Amazon's spread has gained 129%.
Bond yields also remain elevated.
"It's not necessarily fundamentals," said CreditSights analyst Jordan Chalfin. "It's more, I'd say, 80% driven by technicals and sentiment."
Alphabet and Amazon pose the next big hurdle for tech bonds as they update their capex plans and free cash flow forecasts. Microsoft 's earnings are also due Wednesday, but the company has yet to issue any bonds to pay for its AI spending.
Both Amazon and Alphabet reported negative free cash flow in the second quarter and analysts expect that trend to continue.
Analysts expect Alphabet to report free cash flow of -$2.3 billion while spending $55.2 billion on capital expenditures in the third quarter, according to FactSet consensus estimates. Amazon is expected to report -$9.9 billion in free cash flow against capex of $58.7 billion.
S&P Global Ratings estimated in an August report that the hyperscalers will have negative free operating cash flow in 2026 and 2027.
More critical will be their outlooks, Cheng says. "The singular focus on the investors' minds is really what the capex guidance trajectory looks like across the hyperscaler space."
Meeks believes elevated capex is a sign of strong AI demand. The hyperscalers have "decided that with all the evidence they have — and they have more than you and me — that this is worthwhile spending, and not just worthwhile; it's required," he said.
CreditSights' Chalfin doesn't expect the hyperscalers to announce major new bond issuance around their earnings reports. Oracle's updates may be more critical for credit markets. The company has issued $117 billion in long-term debt and is clinging to an investment-grade credit rating of BBB-, the lowest level of investment grade above junk, according to S&P.
"It's the most important IG tech credit, just given how it's a bit more stressed relative to the A-rated names," he said. "It's trading more like a high-yield credit, even though it's IG, and so there's just a lot of investor concern on that one."
One wrinkle to the AI debt story: balance sheets don't reveal the whole picture. The companies are using complicated off-balance sheet arrangements for data centers and chip financing, and they aren't fully transparent, S&P Global said in a September report.
"There are commitments they are entering into, for example, into data center leases or purchase commitments on chips that aren't necessarily treated as debt," Mark Habib, digital infrastructure sector lead at S&P Global Ratings, said on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" Monday.
S&P is trying to provide the market with more visibility on those commitments "to give a fuller picture of what kinds of obligations they're actually entering into," he added.
Oracle aside, hyperscaler credit ratings are all comfortably above A levels — reflecting the fact that they have broadly diversified revenue streams, ample coverage for interest payments, and capacity to add leverage if they choose.
Nuveen's Cheng isn't concerned, pointing out that while there has been some credit repricing, there is no credit crisis.
"They continue to have exceptional credit profiles, strong cash generation liquidity," he said of the largest hyperscalers.
"The market is really not concerned about credit quality at this point," Cheng added. "It's really just the trajectory of the capex needs and the supply of debt to fund that. Both of those are pointing in one direction — and that's up."
Correction: This story has been revised to reflect that Oracle's investment-grade credit rating is BBB-, according to S&P. A previous version mischaracterized the company's credit rating.

articles.title_zh: Report: iPhone 18 Pro sales down 4% in the US, but China drives 3.1% global growth
articles.content_orig:
Counterpoint Research’s latest report offers a look at global iPhone 18 Pro sales during the first three weeks of availability. Here are the details.
In a report released today, Counterpoint Research says iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max sales in the US fell 4% during their first three weeks of availability compared to the first three weeks of iPhone 17 Pro series sales last year.
The report noted that Japan saw a whopping 27% drop in sales, with demand weakening “as exchange rates amplified the price increases.”
China, on the other hand, saw a 29% increase in sales, while other markets collectively recorded a more modest 3.1% increase.
The report doesn’t break down what that means in units, or millions of units, but it does offer some context on what drove these regional differences.
A regional breakdown shows that the global 3.1% growth was concentrated in specific markets. China posted the strongest growth, with sales rising 29% YoY. This was driven by better early supply compared with last year and by price increases on competing flagship models from Chinese Android OEMs. Excluding China’s contribution, the global sales growth rate would have been far weaker. The US and Japan experienced a YoY decline, affected by higher prices compared with their predecessors. In the US, consumers largely do not perceive meaningful improvements over the previous models in either features or design, while in Japan, demand has contracted as exchange rates amplified the price increases.
Today’s report also includes another interesting tidbit: According to Counterpoint, the iPhone 18 Pro Max accounted for a slightly smaller share of Pro-series sales compared to last year’s iPhone 17 Pro series, which the firm attributed to higher prices and stronger demand for the smaller Pro model in emerging markets:
The iPhone 18 Pro Max accounted for 56% of sales within the iPhone 18 Pro series, a slight decrease from 57% last year. This can be attributed to the higher prices compared with last year, as well as the fact that the sales growth in emerging markets such as India and Southeast Asia skewed more toward the Pro models.
As to how, or whether, the iPhone Duo had any effect on these shifting numbers, the report didn’t address that directly, since the device launched after the three-week period covered by the data. However, Counterpoint Associate Director Sujeong Lim raised the possibility that it could affect Pro Max sales going forward:
“Whether China’s outperformance reflects durable demand or front-loaded buying will become clearer in the coming weeks. The recovery of US and Japanese volumes, and whether the iPhone Duo launching in Week 43 will generate incremental demand rather than cannibalising Pro Max, are the two most consequential near-term variables.”

articles.title_orig: Nvidia's worst nightmare may be lurking inside Anthropic's IPO filing
articles.title_zh: Nvidia's worst nightmare may be lurking inside Anthropic's IPO filing
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic is hedging its bets by using multiple chips to handle its AI work — a strategy that could eventually erode Nvidia's dominance.
The AI lab says it manages compute "as a single, fungible pool from multiple strategic partners" — with software that can direct its work to different chips depending on where they're most productive, according to Anthropic's S-1 filing , which came out Monday as the company prepares to go public.
Anthropic says it uses hardware from four chip families: Amazon Trainium, Google TPUs, Nvidia GPUs, and AMD GPUs.
That flexibility, which Anthropic said "took years and significant investment to build," could make major AI companies less dependent on Nvidia over time and give them more negotiating leverage, analysts said.
"The real exposure could be Nvidia's pricing power," said Patrick Moorhead, founder and CEO of Moor Insights & Strategy, "because a customer that can shift work across four platforms negotiates very differently than one that can't."
Ashish Nadkarni, an analyst at IDC, added that a multichip approach also makes Anthropic less vulnerable to fluctuations in Nvidia's chip supply.
Although Anthropic's chip mix isn't new, the company is now pitching it as a core advantage to investors, Moorhead said.
The threat has its limits. Switching between chips is still difficult — especially when it comes to training AI models as opposed to running them, Moorhead said — and only the biggest AI companies have the resources to do it.
Anthropic also continues to spend billions on Nvidia compute , Moorhead said.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson, said that while other major companies like OpenAI likely take a multichip approach, it may not be worth the effort and investment for smaller players.
Brad Gastwirth, global head of research and market intelligence at Circular Technology, said Anthropic's strategy doesn't represent a major near-term threat. Having more chip options doesn't erase Nvidia's advantages in performance, networking, and software, he said.
There's a broader risk for Nvidia if AI compute becomes more of a commodity.
Citadel CEO Ken Griffin has warned that if supply overtakes demand, it could drive down rental prices.
"GPUs, like airlines, have a very low marginal cost to run," he told Bloomberg last week. "The moment you have overcapacity, pricing goes into freefall."
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider.

articles.title_orig: ChatGPT’s Advice to Cut Her Seizure Drug Led to Devastating Consequences
articles.title_zh: ChatGPT’s Advice to Cut Her Seizure Drug Led to Devastating Consequences
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Claims ChatGPT practiced medicine without a license advising Bowen Wan to reduce her anti-seizure medication to zero without telling her doctors, resulting in her death from a preventable seizure
SAN FRANCISCO, October 27, 2026 --( BUSINESS WIRE )--The Social Media Victims Law Center , a legal advocacy organization representing parents of children harmed by social media and AI platforms, and The Schenk Law Firm, LLP, have filed a wrongful death lawsuit on behalf of Bowen Wan's parents, Qun Wan and Meiqin Xu, against OpenAI and its CEO Samuel Altman, alleging that ChatGPT dispensed unlicensed and dangerously inaccurate medical advice to a woman with epilepsy, resulting in the preventable death of Bowen, a 31-year-old prodigy originally from Jiangsu, China, living in Seattle.
According to the complaint, which was filed in the Superior Court of California, City and County of San Francisco, and which is pleaded as an add-on to the coordinated ChatGPT Product Liability Cases (JCCP No. 5431), ChatGPT provided Bowen with dangerously inaccurate medical advice, selected and adjusted her prescriptions, and designed an aggressive tapering schedule to completely stop her use of lamotrigine, the anti-seizure medication keeping her alive and, in doing so, killed her. The complaint alleges that ChatGPT practiced medicine without a license on a patient who was relying on it, explicitly, for medical advice she believed would help her, and who died after it directed her off the medication her physicians had prescribed.
Bowen communicated with ChatGPT in both English and Mandarin. Independent researchers found, before GPT-4o shipped, that OpenAI's models produced unsafe content more than three times as often in Chinese as in English. OpenAI nonetheless invited users everywhere to bring their health questions to ChatGPT in every language, and Bowen brought hers in Chinese.
Time and again, the complaint alleges, after her doctors prescribed her medications, ChatGPT inserted itself between the prescription and the patient. It told Bowen which drugs to refuse, coached her to take doses her doctors had never approved, and supplied the schedules, scripts, and reassurances her physicians never saw. The product worked to keep her doctors out of her care, telling Bowen that her epileptologist "most likely has never encountered your type" and could not understand her condition. When Bowen anticipated her doctors would consider ChatGPT's tapering plan too risky, ChatGPT told her that "a doctor saying it is 'too fast' does not mean you are 'doing it wrong'" and that "the doctor's concerns about 'risk' do not apply to you."
According to the complaint, no warning, in any language, ever told Bowen that the product's accuracy and its safety guardrails were materially weaker in Chinese. Defendants could have returned a categorical warning to every prompt she sent, such as, "I am not a licensed physician. Consult your healthcare provider." Instead, the product did the opposite: when Bowen's physician ordered the blood test that would have revealed her collapsing lamotrigine level, ChatGPT praised her refusal to take the blood test as a "very robust avoidance strategy." OpenAI had already built exactly that kind of unbypassable, categorical guardrail for copyrighted material. It chose not to build one to protect her.
Over the course of twenty-five days, the complaint alleges, ChatGPT "coached" Bowen off lamotrigine, the antiseizure medication that had kept her alive for years. It designed a day-by-day schedule tapering her stable 400-milligram dose to zero. No physician ever prescribed such a regimen, and it directly contradicts the FDA-approved patient medication guide for LAMICTAL (lamotrigine). The complaint alleges that ChatGPT conditioned Bowen to distrust her doctors, instructed her to conceal the taper it created, and effectively installed itself as her de facto medical advisor.
After two days of unsuccessfully trying to reach their daughter, Bowen's parents asked a family friend to enter her Capitol Hill apartment. As they watched anxiously through a live WeChat video stream from 5,700 miles away, the friend stepped inside and walked to Bowen's bedroom, where he found her lying face down in her bed. Their daughter — a computer-science graduate of Arizona State University and a machine-learning software engineer at Amazon — was found dead on Valentine's Day as her parents looked on helplessly from the other side of the world.
Bowen took her last dose of lamotrigine on or about February 10, 2026. The schedule ChatGPT designed fixed February 12 as the day she would be fully off the drug, and, according to the complaint, that is the date she died.
According to the King County Medical Examiner, Bowen died of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP), and her postmortem blood contained lamotrigine at roughly one-fifth of the lowest concentration generally regarded as therapeutic, consistent with a patient who had recently stopped the drug.
"OpenAI built a product that spoke with the confidence of a medical professional but carried none of the training, oversight, or responsibility that real doctors have," said Matthew P. Bergman , founding attorney of the Social Media Victims Law Center. "Bowen trusted ChatGPT because it sounded authoritative — and that trust cost her life. If a human doctor had given Bowen this advice, they would be liable for medical malpractice.
"More than 40 million Americans use ChatGPT for health advice every day. That is a staggering number of people being placed in danger by a product that has no right – and no expertise – to be practicing medicine," he added.
"Bowen's death is what happens when companies race one another and ship a product faster than they can control it. Her medication controlled her epilepsy for years, and people live that way into their eighties. Bowen was thirty-one. The complaint alleges ChatGPT diagnosed Bowen, wrote her a dose-by-dose taper schedule, and revised it when she had seizures. That is practicing medicine. And in California you need a license to do so. This case demands an accounting for the harm that has been done. It asks where generative AI stops and medicine begins, and who answers when a product crosses that line," said Benjamin S. Schenk, Partner, The Schenk Law Firm, LLP.
About the Social Media Victims Law Center
The Social Media Victims Law Center (SMVLC), socialmediavictims.org, was founded in 2021 to hold tech companies legally accountable for the harm they inflict on vulnerable users. SMVLC seeks to apply principles of product liability to force tech companies to elevate consumer safety to the forefront of its economic analysis and design safer products to protect users from foreseeable harm.
About The Schenk Law Firm, LLP
The Schenk Law Firm, LLP is a San Diego-based law firm representing individuals and families nationwide in personal injury, wrongful death, and mass tort cases, including claims against AI companies whose products have caused serious harm to their users. Since 1979, the firm has helped clients recover over $25 billion. Learn more at schenklawfirm.com.

The No. 1 cereal brand* and the No. 1 most trusted food storage brand** bring freshness you can reseal to the cereal aisle – available exclusively at Walmart.com beginning Oct. 27.
MINNEAPOLIS and RACINE, Wis. — Oct. 27, 2026 — You asked, Cheerios™ and Ziploc® Brand delivered – freshness you can reseal! After receiving hundreds of thousands of requests, comments and reactions annually on the topic, Cheerios and Ziploc® Brand have come together to introduce Cheerios with Ziploc PantrySeal™. The new innovation features the first resealable bag inside a traditional cereal box, making it easier to pour, reseal and help keep cereal fresher longer.
The partnership brings together Cheerios, the No. 1 cereal brand*, with more than 50 years of Ziploc® Brand expertise helping people seal in freshness and store the foods they love. It’s a natural pairing for cereal lovers, 90% of whom say they already take extra steps beyond simply closing the cereal box to help preserve freshness*** like folding the bag, rolling it, clipping it or even transferring it to another container.
“General Mills has received letters, emails and DMs asking for an easier way to reseal a cereal box, and we decided it was time to partner with the ultimate freshness brand: Ziploc®,” said Emilie Knox, Vice President and Business Unit Director for Cheerios at General Mills. “Cheerios with Ziploc PantrySeal™ takes a small, everyday cereal frustration and finally gives consumers the simple solution they’ve been asking for, making the whole routine easier and more enjoyable.”
Cheerios with Ziploc PantrySeal™ is made for how people want to pour a bowl of cereal, as well as store it. The resealable bag is designed to open only partially across the top to create a convenient “pour spout” as an easier way for the whole family to fill a bowl (or a cup, mug or even little hands). Cheerios with Ziploc PantrySeal™ then seals closed right inside the box for cereal freshness you can reseal.
“For generations, Ziploc® Brand has helped people keep the foods they love fresh through simple, trusted solutions,” said a Ziploc® Brand spokesperson. “Cheerios with Ziploc PantrySeal™ is an exciting new expression of what Ziploc® Brand can do – bringing our resealable freshness expertise directly into the Cheerios package and Ziploc® Brand into the pantry in an entirely new way.”
Available as a new option in the cereal aisle for both Cheerios and Honey Nut Cheerios, Cheerios with Ziploc PantrySeal™ combines the same Cheerios families already reach for with Ziploc® Brand’s expertise in resealable storage, for an easier way to open, pour, reseal – and keep enjoying.
A fix that feels this intuitive was anything but simple. With nearly one box of Cheerios produced every second, the new Cheerios with Ziploc PantrySeal™ had to be developed to work at Cheerios scale while keeping the same familiar cereal flowing to pantries nationwide. For Ziploc® Brand, the partnership builds on a history of resealable storage that began with the introduction of its innovative zipper technology in 1968.
And there’s a fitting full-circle connection: Cheerios with Ziploc PantrySeal™ is being produced exclusively in Buffalo, New York, in the same place where Cheerios was first made in 1941.
Cheerios with Ziploc PantrySeal™ is now available exclusively at Walmart.com and will roll out to retailers nationwide in the coming months.

articles.title_orig: Google begins certifying Registered App Stores for Android, but not in the US
articles.title_zh: Google begins certifying Registered App Stores for Android, but not in the US
articles.content_orig:
Running an app ecosystem has gotten a lot more complex for Google after its loss in the Epic Games antitrust case. While US users can access app stores in Google Play by court order, international users will use Google’s voluntary Registered App Stores program . Google has announced that stores wishing to be part of that program are now free to apply, and support will roll out to some Android devices later this year.
App stores accepted into the program will enjoy preferential treatment on the Android platform. Users of approved stores will be able to install apps with a single click, similar to the experience in the Play Store. These stores will also be allowed to update apps silently in the background like Google’s store does.
“In March, we announced the Registered App Stores program to give third-party app stores a more streamlined way to reach users while maintaining the safety and security of the Android ecosystem,” said a Google spokesperson. “Eligible app stores outside the US can now apply to register their stores ahead of the new simplified installation experience rolling out to users later this year.”
The Android Registered App Stores program was initially Google’s backup plan. After losing its appeal of Judge James Donato’s verdict, Google was faced with a number of remedies, like allowing third-party billing and sharing app catalogs with rival stores. The most dramatic shift was the court’s requirement that Google distribute third-party stores within Google Play.
Google and Epic, having patched things up following the trial, attempted to settle the case in a way that gave Google more control. Registered App Stores were intended as a replacement for hosting the stores in Google Play, provided they could adhere to a baseline level of trust and safety. Google intended to use this program in the US and internationally, but the companies withdrew the settlement when the court signaled it would not be approved.
Registered App Stores are still happening on Android, but they won’t be supported in the US—you can go to Google Play for alternative stores stateside, but so far, Aptoide remains the only one listed . Those operating Android app storefronts who want to be included in the international program can now review the program and begin the enrollment process.
Any store hoping to get approval will have to adhere to a number of requirements , including protecting intellectual property, removing illegal content, and publishing a privacy policy for both users and developers. Google also requires several ongoing security measures to ensure the stores do not give malware easier access to Android devices. As part of the application process, store operators must provide documentation for all these points (in English) and upload copies of all their apps.
It costs $10,000 per year to participate in the Android Registered App Stores program, and that fee must be paid before Google will review the application. Google says this fee covers the additional support necessary to run the program. There may also be additional review fees if Google detects a store has a problem with malware.
Google plans to roll out support in dozens of nations , which includes most of the world outside of the US and Europe. The program goes live on December 1, but it will only work on Android devices running the latest builds of Android 17. Google says support will start with Android 17 QPR2, which is expected to arrive on Pixel phones in the coming weeks. Google doesn’t even sell those in most of the supported regions, and the devices people do use in such places tend to have much slower updates. A substantial number of Android devices in supported countries may never even see an update compatible with the Registered App Stores program.

articles.title_orig: Why Anthropic's IPO contrasts the 'cult of Elon Musk' at SpaceX and Tesla
articles.title_zh: Why Anthropic's IPO contrasts the 'cult of Elon Musk' at SpaceX and Tesla
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
In the first mega IPO of 2026, SpaceX ( SPCX ) singled out one person in its prospectus as the shot caller: none other than the world's richest person, Elon Musk.
The next big IPO of the year — Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ), which could be the largest of all time — is run more by a committee of founders. That's a good thing given its mission and structures, according to veteran dealmaker Jim Neeson.
"I would say having seven founders working together can make it where it's not just like a cult of Elon Musk, right?" the Connor Group founding executive said on Sozzi Unleashed . "You actually have it where you have a consortium of people making decisions, which I actually think can be a good thing."
Neeson noted that Anthropic is a public benefit company with seven founders who collectively own 50.1%.
"You have a board that will be approved by sort of a trust fund. And then you also have a business where it's not just going to be about profits. It's also going to be sort of the social benefit piece that's built into their doctrine," he explained.
Anthropic's founders are CEO Dario Amodei and his sister and president, Daniela Amodei, as well as Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Chris Olah. The consortium left OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ) to start Anthropic in January 2021.
The seven co-founders will be issued new Class F common stock as part of the IPO, giving them majority control of the company — something Neeson said investors will have to navigate.
"If you look at Meta, [and] you also look at Google, you had very strong founders," Neeson said. "A lot of times that is the venture capital case. I want founders that can make strong decisions and not be beholden to sort of quarterly type of trends."
"This is going to be a different type of structure out there, and it's going to be tested," he added. "We've never seen it, especially at this scale, especially at these growth rates. So I would say that's one thing analysts and investors are going to be looking very closely at."
The group looks to be managing the financials relatively well.
Anthropic's first-half 2026 revenue surged to $16.3 billion from $1.1 billion a year earlier, the prospectus showed. The filing also discloses an $80.7 billion first-half net loss, a strong signal of aggressive AI spending in the years ahead.
On an adjusted basis, Anthropic posted $1.62 billion in operating income through the first six months of 2026 compared to a loss of $1.85 billion last year.
Investment bankers are reportedly aiming for an astronomical listing valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion.
Anthropic could debut on public markets before the end of November. It plans to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.

articles.title_orig: Oil Futures Fall as Market Holds Out Hope for Middle East Diplomacy
articles.title_zh: Oil Futures Fall as Market Holds Out Hope for Middle East Diplomacy
articles.content_orig:
Oil prices tumbled on Monday morning as diplomatic efforts to calm the Iran war gathered pace and US President Donald Trump said he was weighing a deal with Tehran.
Brent, the global oil benchmark, fell more than 6% from about $117.4 per barrel at Friday’s close to around $110 at the time of writing, while US benchmark West Texas Intermediate dropped about 2% to $101.5 per barrel.
Friday's close was Brent’s highest since 19 March and only about 2% below the $119.5 peak hit in early March, at the start of the Iran war. Before the conflict, Brent traded at around $72 per barrel.
Prices had surged last week after Yemen's Houthi rebels, an Iran-aligned armed group, attacked airports and energy facilities in Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest oil exporter.
However, the mood shifted over the weekend.
Qatari mediators reportedly travelled to Tehran on Sunday in coordination with Washington, while Saudi Arabia's defence minister, Pakistan's army chief and Turkey's intelligence chief were due in the Iranian capital on Monday for regional security talks.
In an interview with Fox News on Sunday, Trump framed it as a choice asking, "do I make a deal with them, or do I finish them off?"
Supply risks have not gone away as the Houthis said they struck Saudi airports and energy sites again over the weekend, while Riyadh reported shooting down further missiles and drones.
At a campaign event in Port Huron, Michigan, ahead of the US midterm elections, Trump defended his administration's reasons for starting the conflict.
Citing the Wall Street Journal, he also claimed that "oil coming out of the Strait of Hormuz is now topping what it was before the war [...] our navy has been incredible."
The Strait of Hormuz carried about a fifth of the world’s oil before the war.
Gulf crude exports, excluding Iran, returned to pre-war levels in September, according to ship-tracking firm Kpler, but around 40% of them now bypass the strait through pipelines, compared with 17% before the conflict.
Investors are also bracing for a busy week of rate decisions from the world's major central banks.
In Europe, both the pan-European Stoxx 600 and the Euro Stoxx 50 traded over 0.6% higher than Friday's close.
The UK's FTSE 100, Germany's DAX, France's CAC 40, Italy's FTSE MIB and Switzerland's SMI, all rose between 0.3% and 1% with the German index leading.
Spain’s IBEX 35 and the Netherlands’ AEX both traded flat.
French assets got some relief after ratings agency Moody’s unexpectedly kept France’s Aa3 rating on Friday evening.
In the US, futures on the S&P 500 were 0.3% higher and those on the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 as well.
The week ahead is packed as the US Federal Reserve announces its decision on Wednesday, and is widely expected to keep rates at 3.75% to 4% before a possible hike in December.
The European Central Bank follows on Thursday, with France's bond market turmoil in focus, and the Bank of Japan on Friday.
Earnings season also peaks, with roughly one in three S&P 500 firms reporting, Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon among them, while BP and Shell update investors in Europe.

articles.title_orig: The Trump admin said energy costs were a small price to pay in Iran war, but U.S. consumers are paying nearly 8x more than anyone else in fuel costs
articles.title_zh: The Trump admin said energy costs were a small price to pay in Iran war, but U.S. consumers are paying nearly 8x more than anyone else in fuel costs
articles.content_orig:
The Iran war continues to weigh on Americans’ wallets, and it’s costing them more in increased fuel costs than consumers in any other country in the world, new data finds. As President Donald Trump argues the cost of the war will be justified with economic prosperity, his administration may be pushing policies making the problem worse.
U.S. consumers have paid an average of $471 more in fuel prices since the beginning of the Iran war in February, according to a report published on Monday by Finland-based nonprofit research institute Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA). That’s nearly eight times greater than the average of about $60 in increased energy costs per person globally. As a country, the U.S. has spent $160 billion total on increased fuel costs since the beginning of the war, with China following at $54 billion, and Canada coming in third at $17 billion.
The Iran war has cost U.S. households about $2,000 , according to Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, a sum that includes both soaring prices at the gas pump as well as increased airfares and inflation as a result of increased transportation expenses and supply-chain shuffles over the last seven months of Middle East turmoil.
Trump has repeatedly tried to assuage Americans’ anxieties about increased costs associated with the war. At a rally in North Carolina in September, the president downplayed affordability concerns . He has argued the war is necessary to prevent Iran from attaining nuclear weapons, and that the U.S. is making a “ freaking fortune ” as a result of increased energy production.
“It’s a very inexpensive price to pay for what we’ve done,” Trump said last month of fuel costs, which have now topped $4.26 per gallon, up from $2.98 before the war. “Remember that.”
The White House did not immediately respond to Fortune ’s request for comment.
To be sure, the Iran war did not create the conditions under which American consumers in particular are paying higher energy costs. While global supply strains have increased fuel prices globally, the outsize impact on U.S. consumers is a result of an American economy and culture structured around oil.
“If you compare the U.S. with countries in Europe with similar levels of income, you can really see the effect of decades of lower prices for fuel and less emphasis on sustainable transportation,” CREA cofounder and report author Lauri Myllyvirta told Fortune . “Undoing that, of course, takes quite a bit of time and effort.”
The U.S. is heavily exposed to higher fuel costs in part because it is beholden to global market rates, a result of it still having to trade for heavy oil despite being a major diesel producer. But the heavier energy burden on American consumers is mostly because of the country’s reliance on oil over other sustainable means of energy, CREA argued.
The U.S. has less electric-vehicle adoption than other countries. And less efficient gas-powered cars travel farther on American roads compared to other countries, meaning American consumers simply burn more fuel than consumers in other countries, the report said. CREA found a positive correlation between countries with the greatest EV market share—Norway, Sweden, Finland, the Netherlands, and Belgium—and fuel cost savings per person.
Across the world, EV sales have surged as fuel costs have increased. In Denmark, for example, EVs made up 81% of new-vehicle sales in the first eight months of 2026. Nearly all new-vehicle sales in Norway over the same period were EVs, and 57% of new-vehicle sales in China were all-electric. Some European countries such as Germany saw a decrease in gas and diesel demand in 2026.
By comparison, only 7.3% of new-vehicle sales in the U.S. over that span were plug-in EVs, and the report found that American drivers who made the switch to eclectic cars saw only a $17 increase in charging costs since early March as a result of electricity price increases.
Myllyvirta suggested this pattern is primed to continue. A series of U.S. policy changes has disincentivized Americans from purchasing EVs and automakers from building fuel efficient vehicles.
The Trump administration ended a $7,500 tax credit on new EVs in September 2025 it claimed would devastate the auto industry. Analysts have cited the end of the incentive as the reason EV demand flattened in the U.S., and the reason why companies like Ford rolled back production on all-electric cars in favor of hybrid vehicles.
Last month, Trump released new fuel economy standards , loosening Biden-era regulatory requirements for fuel efficiency to mitigate pollution—a move the president said would make cars more affordable, but that environmentalists argued would drive up fuel costs and cancel out any vehicle savings.
According to Myllyvirta, increased fuel costs for Americans are poised to continue, even if the war ends. While energy prices will level out once this conflict is over, the reliance on gas-powered cars will mean a repetition of this cycle during the next energy shock.
“The only certainty is volatility,” he said. “Prices are going to come down, and then there are going to be new shocks. And as long as the reliance on oil continues, that cycle is going to play out with effects on consumers, with effects on inflation and economic policy.”
Sasha Rogelberg is a reporter and former editorial fellow on the news desk at Fortune , covering retail and the intersection of business and popular culture.

articles.title_orig: Deaths in detention cells in Nigeria were entirely preventable, inquiry finds
articles.title_zh: Deaths in detention cells in Nigeria were entirely preventable, inquiry finds
articles.content_orig:
The BBC's Madina Maishanu shows the conditions inside the cell where so many died
An inquiry into the deaths of 33 detainees in Nigeria's Minna state has found they died as a result of severe overcrowding, poor ventilation and failure by officers to respond to distress calls.
Forensic and medical evidence showed the "entirely preventable" deaths had resulted from acute respiratory failure linked to prolonged confinement, aggravated by heat stress and dehydration.
The evidence did not support initial claims of a disease outbreak.
The detainees were found dead on 17 September while being held by the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps on suspicion of illegal mining. The investigation found that the mining sites had been licensed.
'I have never felt heat like that' - a survivor on watching 33 cellmates die in Nigeria
Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo said those found responsible for the deaths would face the full force of the law.
He added that the detention hall had been cleaned before investigators arrived, raising concerns about possible attempts to compromise evidence.
Implicated officers will face suspension and the report would be forwarded to the attorney general of the federation for further legal action, Tunji-Ojo said.
Family members reclaimed the bodies of their relatives from Minna's General Hospital last month
The investigating committee found that the raid on the miners had been conducted without an approved operational order, proper planning or consultation with the Mining Marshals Unit.
It said that 50 detainees had been held in a cell measuring about 20 sq m, with no running water or functioning toilet, and inadequate food, drinking water and airflow.
Adults and minors were detained together, and some detainees were held beyond lawful detention periods.
Officers reportedly ignored repeated calls for help, despite a medical worker having raised concerns about the conditions.
"Detainees repeatedly banged on cell doors and walls, shouted for assistance and pleaded for water," said the head of the investigating team, Jonathan Kure.
"These distress calls were heard by officers assigned to nearby duties... but were not acted upon."
Kure said the detention conditions amounted to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment.
"The tragedy demonstrates the consequences of systemic disregard for detention standards, supervisory responsibilities and the welfare of persons in custody," he added.
The investigating committee also recommended compensation of 30m naira (Â£16,683; $22,285) for each of the bereaved families and 10m naira for each survivor.

articles.title_orig: Amazon's anti-tokenmaxxing memo says engineers should be pickier about using AI
articles.title_zh: Amazon's anti-tokenmaxxing memo says engineers should be pickier about using AI
articles.content_orig:
Amazon laid out its AI usage guidelines for software engineers in a memo to staffers, and discouraged employees from turning to "tokenmaxxing" in their push to embrace artificial intelligence tools.
The memo , which was circulated internally in September and posted to the company's website on Tuesday, revises how the company defines the role of software development engineers and managers in the age of AI.
"We're just seeing the beginning of AI's effect on software engineering," the company wrote. "While we have a vision for what the future looks like, there's a lot that's still emerging. We are certain that whatever future best practices are, AI will be at the center of software engineering practice."
Under CEO Andy Jassy , Amazon has rapidly integrated AI across the company's sprawling business operations. Jassy has previously predicted that AI will "change the scope and speed" of day-to-day work, and potentially shrink its corporate workforce in the next few years through automation, though he's noted it will also create "other jobs."
As employees rush to adopt AI tools, companies have grappled with the technology's surging costs and how to reliably measure whether the technology leads to a productivity boost or other valuable returns on investment.
Companies have recently cracked down on tokenmaxxing , in which developers use AI as much as possible with little regard for output. Some companies have set limits on employees' usage of tokens, or the units of data that are processed and generated by AI models, in a bid to slow rising AI bills. Others have switched to cheaper, open-source models for certain tasks.
An Amazon spokesperson said the company hasn't instituted caps on employees' token usage. Amazon in May shut down an internal leaderboard after discovering employees were tokenmaxxing to climb the ranks.
In the memo posted Tuesday, Amazon said metrics like token usage, the rate of adoption of AI tools, and code changes or reviews remain "deeply flawed" ways of measuring teams or organizations' AI usage, adding that they can lead to higher costs and too much complexity.
It stopped short of telling staffers to ignore those metrics altogether, however. Token usage and code generation should be considered "with care and judgment" alongside other data, Amazon said.
"We believe that it is best to measure, and be measured by, long-term outcomes," the company wrote.
Marc Brooker, a vice president and distinguished engineer at Amazon Web Services, told CNBC in an interview that the company has looked to metrics such as "feature velocity" to measure how AI is improving engineer productivity.
The metric looks at things like, "how many launches are we doing, how many successful changes are we making in production," he said.
"Broadly, we think about this as a return on investment," Brooker said. "If there is an important problem to solve for our customers, important problem to solve for our business, we're going to invest tools, time, tokens, human effort, etc. into those."
He added, "What we don't want to see is wasted effort where we are going and spending those tokens solving problems that don't matter and sometimes it's hard to know, so we do need to have some appetite for experimentation."
Amazon also discouraged staffers from using AI when it doesn't make sense for a given task.
"If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing," Amazon said in the memo.
The company added, "An engineer who can explain where AI does not yet help their work is demonstrating the judgement we are asking for."

articles.title_orig: Amid the Anthropic IPO excitement, don't forget about earnings season
articles.title_zh: Amid the Anthropic IPO excitement, don't forget about earnings season
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
We are only two days into the week, and it already feels like it should be the weekend.
In the past two days, Meta ( META ) said it will raise $95 billion to support its AI build-out through stock offerings, and Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) dropped a 407-page IPO prospectus that I know you haven't read in its entirety. (Wall Street hasn't either, so don't lose sleep over it.)
Lost in that activity is that earnings season continues in full swing, with results from Coca-Cola ( KO ), Hilton ( HLT ), UPS ( UPS ), Whirlpool ( WHR ), and others today.
While investors are jacked up about AI and some stability returning to the tech trade, don't lose sight of earnings season: After all, it's earnings and earnings expectations that power stocks, not Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei (although his comments have moved markets in the past).
So here are a few quick takes on a couple of earnings reports I chewed through this morning:
I don't have any problems with this Hilton quarter, even though the stock is getting hit on a slight revenue miss. The important revenue per available room metric grew 5.8%, the company remains an aggressive buyer of its stock, and it approved the development of 30,500 rooms in the quarter.
The report fits nicely with the Delta ( DAL ) report we got last week, in that higher fuel prices don't appear to be slowing leisure or business travelers.
I think it also fits nicely with the numbers out of UPS today, with US sales up 4.5% and its full-year guidance hike.
Coca-Cola's latest guidance lift reinforces the view that the company continues to take massive market share away from rival PepsiCo ( PEP ). Coke Zero sales surged 16%.
Not a good day for the team at PepsiCo up in Purchase, N.Y.
I continue to be absolutely shocked by what's happening at Whirlpool ( WHR ). Another supersoft quarter, with an adjusted loss of $0.21 per share. Costs are up, and the business is being hurt by a near-frozen US housing market.
You need nerves of steel to buy Whirlpool shares here — the stock is down more than 63% this year. If you do, the thesis has to be that the iconic company is acquired at some point in the next 12 months.

articles.title_orig: Weil Gotshal Enlists Bankruptcy Lawyer, as Firm’s Situation Worsens
articles.title_zh: Weil Gotshal Enlists Bankruptcy Lawyer, as Firm’s Situation Worsens
articles.content_orig:
The partner set to take over leadership of Weil, Gotshal & Manges has held talks to leave the firm for a rival, a move that would compound ongoing talent drain at one of Wall Streetâs top dealmaking and restructuring shops.
Ramona Nee, Weilâs co-managing partner, has had discussions to join Simpson Thacher & Bartlett, according to people familiar with the matter. Nee, an adviser to big private equity firms including Advent, was slated to take over as Weilâs sole chair in January.
Weil declined to comment. Nee did not return a request for comment. Her departure is not guaranteed and the talks could fall apart, the people said.
If she does leave, she would follow a flood of Weilâs top talent out the door and the breakdown of merger talks with crosstown rival Willkie Farr & Gallagher. Rainmaker Michael Aiello defected to Cravath, Swaine & Moore with a team of partners. It would be likely that a sizable portion of Weilâs Boston partnership would leave with her, according to one person familiar with the matter who is close with many of Weilâs top Boston lawyers.
Nee had told Weil partners she would not take the chair job, which was announced last spring, according to a person briefed on the communication. The Financial Times earlier reported that decision.
Remaining and former Weil lawyers place blame on Aielloâs departure â and Neeâs possible departure â at the feet of executive partner Barry Wolf, who has helmed the firm to some success for more than a decade but in recent years has failed to convince senior partners that Weil has a vision for a world where AI and outsize pay packages upend the perceived usefulness of high-end legal advice.
Aielloâs departure came as a result, in part, because top Weil leaders including Wolf failed to lay out a convincing long-term vision for the firm, according to a person familiar with his thinking.

articles.title_orig: The secret succession rankings that Anthropic shareholders will never see (unless the company is ordered)
articles.title_zh: The secret succession rankings that Anthropic shareholders will never see (unless the company is ordered)
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic has devised an unusual way for its founders to pass on their power.
In its IPO filings , Anthropic outlined how seven of its cofounders, who collectively have 50.1% of voting control, will be able to create a ranked list of who they'd like to inherit their power in the event of their death or incapacitation.
What's particularly notable is that while the names would be shared with the other LLC members and Anthropic's Nominating Committee, they are otherwise contractually confidential and generally not public.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei , Anthropic President Daniela Amodei, and the five other LLC members will review and vote on whether to approve their fellow founders' proposed successors, but the names will likely never be seen by other shareholders. (The agreement allows for the publication only in narrow circumstances, such as a court order or other legal requirement.)
Under the agreement, which was first highlighted by Forbes , each member of the Founders LLC may name up to 10 potential successors, ranked in order of preference. The other LLC members must then vote to approve the secret lists.
While succession plans are not unusual, Anthropic's approach is unusual in how it ranks potential successors. It also underscores how, thanks to the Founders LLC, Anthropic's leaders will be able to maintain control as shareholders begin to offer input post-IPO.
Facebook's 2012 IPO paperwork suggested that if Mark Zuckerberg were in control of the company at the time of his death, then control could be transferred to someone he designated. (Meta has since tweaked this plan.) In 2020, Airbnb's three cofounders agreed to transfer their voting power to their other cofounders if one of them died or became disabled, but that arrangement (which still exists) only lasts for nine months.
The succession plan does not establish CEO succession. Anthropic's board of directors would handle such a chief executive appointment.
There are also some limitations to who the Anthropic founders can name on their lists.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Eight of their 10 potential successors are subject to eligibility requirements, including that the person named is a current or former employee of Anthropic or one of its subsidiaries, or has worked for "a 501(c)(3) tax-exempt organization or a national or international organization whose primary purpose is research, education, or the promotion of public benefit." In either case, the person must have worked there for at least three years.
If the person worked for Anthropic, they must have held a specific role, such as a member of the technical staff or the company's internal think tank, or another role approved by the board and a majority of the other members. If they worked outside Anthropic, they must have held a senior role at the nonprofit. These successors must also be US citizens, have permanent residency, or have valid work authorization.
The other two names, if a founder names all 10 potential successors, are not subject to the eligibility requirements, but they must also receive the required approval.
The succession plan doesn't last forever.
Under the agreement, a successor member generally would cease to be a member on the 10th anniversary of Anthropic's IPO. After that point, successor designees may be admitted only in limited circumstances during a transition period.

articles.title_orig: US Army looks to high-flying balloons to help see, strike along front lines with China
articles.title_zh: US Army looks to high-flying balloons to help see, strike along front lines with China
articles.content_orig:
To burst China’s anti-access/area-denial bubble, the U.S. Army is looking at using high-flying balloons with payloads that can monitor the battlefield, relay communications and strike adversaries.
The Army has tinkered with high-altitude balloons for some time, but interest and experimentation have grown in recent years. Against China’s growing arsenal in the vastness of the Pacific , those balloons could provide a cheaper, lower-signature platform that can be employed from dispersed positions, Maj. Gen. Bernard Harrington, commander of the Army’s 7th Infantry Division/Multi-Domain Command-Pacific, or MDC-P, said at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual conference in Washington, D.C., earlier this month.
Harrington’s command was recently established to merge the ground-maneuver elements of the 7th Infantry Division and long-range capabilities of the 1st Multi-Domain Task Force. Part of the unit’s mission is to operate in space, cyberspace and the electromagnetic spectrum and use long-range fires to help the rest of the Joint Force maneuver, including by opening gaps in China’s anti-access/area-denial network — the air, sea and land-based sensors and weapons designed to keep U.S. forces at bay.
“For us in the Pacific, we really are looking at a specific pacing threat and an anti-access/area-denial network,” against which MDC-P aims to create “windows of opportunity for that Joint Force, whether it be a carrier strike group that’s going to pulse into the weapons engagement zone , whether it be a bomber task force, whether it be a ground unit doing a joint forcible-entry operation,” Harrington said.
High-altitude balloons, or HABs, could facilitate that by carrying “launched effects” — the Army’s term for an aerial system deployed from crewed and uncrewed vehicles for reconnaissance, communications, strikes and other missions. HABs would give MDC-P soldiers more ways to employ attack drones and munitions that are cheaper than “exquisite” missiles, available in greater numbers and harder for adversaries to spot.
Interest in HABs has grown in part due to technological improvements that allow them to stay aloft for weeks or months at a time and give operators more control over where they go. That enhances balloons’ value as platforms for radars and other sensors which, at operating altitudes above 60,000 feet, can see far into rival territory while remaining in international airspace. They also offer a cost-effective complement to satellites, which are more expensive and whose orbits limit their time over any one area.
Harrington described high-altitude balloons as part of “an ecosystem” of data-collecting assets in space, in the air, on land and at sea. HABs in particular could compensate if space-based assets are taken out , Harrington said. “So our ability to employ HABs [and] have HABs be persistent enables both our collection and targeting as well as us [to] provide that information to the Joint Force for their collection and targeting.”
Harrington also described a role for balloon- or unmanned surface vessel-launched effects in kinetic strikes. With the right timing and enough precision, those strikes may not even need to eliminate their target to create an opening.
“Maybe I don’t necessarily need to sink a ship, but if I take out certain systems on that vessel, well, then it creates this temporal window of opportunity,” Harrington said.
“We saw great value [in] that maybe I don’t have to use specifically or unmask an exquisite system to achieve that effect. If I can achieve effect of mass utilizing lower-cost systems, maybe that will get me there,” Harrington added. “So we modeled that, and what we saw was — particularly with our unmanned surface vessels, long-range one-way attack, long-range launched effects — the ability to synchronize and mass that could potentially get us to achieve that effect.”
Harrington’s command experimented with some of those systems during Bayonet Quest 26, an exercise held in Michigan and on Lake Huron from late September to early October. An official video showed soldiers working with air and maritime drones, including a quadcopter launched from a surface vessel and a fixed-wing drone hooked up to a balloon. Harrington said Bayonet Quest tested MDC-P’s ability to “orchestrate those systems” by launching them, gathering data from their sensors, and using AI and LLMs to process that data and produce tasking orders.
“If you see [a potential target], then task a UAS to be able to come over and actually validate if that meets the target folder,” Harrington said, describing the approach. “Then I can task long-range one-way attack [or] an attack USV to be able to achieve that effect or I could send that as a potential fire mission to a more exquisite munition to be able to close that kill chain.”
That reduces the need for a large, easily targetable ground presence, Harrington added: “This is all about integration: Integrate multiple systems into one data layer, be able to lay something like a large language model on top of it, and allow orchestration so we don’t have a lot of soldiers in fixed sites on ground control stations.”
Harrington’s comments come amid a flurry of HAB-related experiments by the Army in North Africa , the Middle East , Europe and the Pacific.
At exercise Valiant Shield in Guam this summer, soldiers experimented with HABs and launched effects “within an island-chain operational construct.” One test sent a HAB aloft towing a long-endurance drone “to evaluate stratospheric payload deployment capabilities.” Soldiers tested the same balloon-drone combo in Japan during Orient Shield in September.
The Army’s Multi-Domain Command-Europe has done dozens of HAB launches over the past year to examine the logistics of employing balloons and to test sensing and communications capabilities using “ experimental payloads .”
Speaking alongside Harrington this month, MDC-E commander Brig. Gen. Steven Carpenter said HABs have a role, alongside other sensors and weapons, in opening “windows of opportunity” against anti-access/area-denial networks, in particular by providing resilient communications and additional strike platforms.
“We like to proliferate the stratosphere with high-altitude balloons, but I mean 200, 300 at a time. We like to use them as drones, [communications retransmission], electromagnetic sensing, electronic attack, and then to drop them down and have air-launched effects,” Carpenter said. “During different seasons, the flight paths are different. We study that. We understand during what seasons, where the best places are to launch those high-altitude systems and then, again, to hold enemy cities and capabilities at risk at any time.”

articles.title_orig: Flávio Bolsonaro's passports cancelled after he fails to surrender them
articles.title_zh: Flávio Bolsonaro's passports cancelled after he fails to surrender them
articles.content_orig:
Far-right senator banned from leaving country as supreme court judge’s ruling cites money-laundering case
The far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro was banned from leaving Brazil and ordered to surrender his passports just hours after his dramatic loss in the presidential election to the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva .
The ruling was issued by Alexandre de Moraes, the same supreme court justice who oversaw the trial of the senator’s father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, for attempting a coup.
Bolsonaro posted a video saying the decision was based on an interview his brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, gave last Friday urging his brother to leave Brazil if he lost the election.
On Monday night, Bolsonaro’s party issued a statement acknowledging the election result, saying: “We recognise the presidential result proclaimed by the electoral court, but believe that the questions raised need to be properly clarified through a balanced and democratic political debate.”
Bolsonaro, like his father four years ago, has still not conceded defeat to Lula.
The court’s brief ruling regarding his passport only refers to a criminal case in which the federal police are investigating Flávio Bolsonaro over his possible involvement in a money-laundering scheme . The ruling orders him not to have any contact with his friend Willer Tomaz, a lawyer linked to betting companies that police suspect were being used to launder about £680m.
It also cancelled all of Bolsonaro’s passports, including the diplomatic one he holds as a congressman, and ordered him to hand them over within 24 hours.
Bolsonaro was the first to speak publicly about the matter, before Brazilian media were even aware of the judge’s decision.
In a video posted on social media, he said he had just left a visit to his father, who is under house arrest in Brasília, when “Lula’s federal police were at his door and in the middle of the street, and I was served with an order to hand over my passports and I am also prohibited from leaving the country”.
He added that, although his brother – who is in self-imposed exile in the US – told a US podcast on Friday that he favoured the senator leaving Brazil if he lost the election, “I never said that”.
When his Senate term ends early next year, Bolsonaro will be out of public office for the first time in 24 years, and therefore without the special immunity afforded to officeholders.
He is under investigation in another criminal case, too, over what happened to the £20m he was captured on tape asking a disgraced banker accused of corruption to provide for a biopic about his father.
The Folha de S Paulo newspaper reported that Flávio Bolsonaro had been persuaded to drop his plan to seek to annul the election, which he had announced after the result was declared on Sunday night.
Bolsonaro had claimed that the two-hour extension of voting – intended to allow voters who had been unable to access the mandatory free public transport to cast their ballots – had harmed the election, despite the fact that his own campaign had also argued for an extension.
According to the newspaper, allies and lawyers told him his argument was legally weak.
Bolsonaro had still not publicly reversed his demand for an annulment, and in the same video he said he would file another case to have Lula’s ticket disqualified over alleged abuse of economic power, a similar case to others his legal team brought during the campaign.

The Dallas-based investment firm Disruptive, whose past bets include Palantir, Airbnb, and Spotify, announced a $10 billion fund to back at least 10 late-stage companies, with checks of up to $1 billion, it said Tuesday .
It’s one of the biggest fundraises of the year so far, aiming to back (what else?!) the capital-intensive fields of AI and defense. The Wall Street Journal first reported earlier this month that the firm was seeking to raise the fund and by then had already secured at least $7.5 billion in capital commitments.
The firm was founded in 2012 by Alex Davis, grandson of billionaire oil magnate Marvin Davis.
This is technically the firm’s first blind-pool fund, meaning investors commit money without knowing which companies it will back. Until now, the firm raised money through deal-by-deal special purpose vehicles . Disruptive has nonetheless made headlines in recent years for pouring money into companies like chip startup Groq and the AI voice-generation startup ElevenLabs. Bloomberg reported that the firm told LPs it has returned more than $6 billion on the roughly $1.9 billion it has put into startups.
According to the Dallas Business Journal, the new vehicle is the largest venture fund raised in Texas history.
